articles.title: ‘We’re not asking for luxury’: school protesters in Paris suburb feel abandoned by French state
articles.summary:
Students say they are desperate to get back to class but conditions are so bad that the protests must continue

On a normal school day, Mohammed, 17, wakes at 6am, cares for his younger…

blocks.text: On a normal school day, Mohammed, 17, wakes at 6am, cares for his younger siblings to help his single mother who works as a security guard, then takes two crowded buses and a local train to get to his high school in Sevran, a low-income banlieue town in the suburbs north-east of Paris.

“There aren’t enough chairs or desks to go round, so some students have to stand up,” Mohammed said. “Classes can be so packed you can’t interact with the teacher. In this year’s heatwaves, it felt like 40 degrees in overcrowded classrooms with no shade or curtains. It was so hot my brain couldn’t function.”

The 17-year-old in his last year of high school wants to study management and digital communication at a Paris university. But he said conditions were so poor, he felt all odds were stacked against him and his classmates.

“Some of us have to go months without teachers when absent staff aren’t replaced,” he said. “One class had no French teacher for several months just before the French baccalaureate, so they couldn’t even study all the set texts for their exam. Recently we needed a teacher for a subject taught through English, but when that teacher arrived they didn’t speak English.”

The biggest youth protest movement in the country in decades brought hundreds of thousands on to the streets across France this week demonstrating against inequality in the French education system, decrepit schools, a lack of teachers and large class sizes. Hundreds of schools were blockaded, thousands of teenagers were arrested, and rights groups warned of alleged police brutality, with one child losing the use of eye and another losing a hand.

Mohammed and his classmates, often supported by their parents and teachers, have been at the frontline, barricading their school, the Lycée Blaise-Cendrars, which is in one of mainland France’s poorest départements, Seine-Saint-Denis. They have voted to continue their protests next week, taking their grievances to the local mayor, elected officials and education representatives. Many local politicians have supported their demands. Even the French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, conceded that teenagers had “legitimate” concerns.

Photos on the Sevran students’ phones showed broken classroom chairs, holes in walls, holes in ceilings, mould, buckets to catch leaks, faulty lights. They said basic needs weren’t met, with some toilets broken, others with no doors and often no toilet paper or soap. Video projectors and science equipment were lacking.

blocks.caption: A student shows an example of conditions in the school on their phone. Photograph: Ed Alcock/The Guardian

blocks.text: “We’re not asking for luxury, just the basics to learn in decent conditions,” Mohammed said. “And yet police on horseback charged us when we were gathered to protest outside our school, firing teargas at us and making arrests. It’s so dangerous to be charged by a horse, it could kill you. I just ran, I was trying to help my classmates.”

The high schools of Seine-Saint-Denis, a suburban area nudging against northern Paris, have been a driving force in the protests. The area has the youngest population in mainland France, one of the highest birthrates and the among the lowest average income. Local high schools have a high turnover of young teachers.

Despite co-hosting the 2024 Paris Olympics, and numerous government plans to try to combat long-running problems of inequality and poverty, the area north-east of Paris is still disadvantaged compared with the capital.

In 2005, Seine-Saint-Denis was the starting point for weeks of unrest on housing estates across France, leading to a state of national emergency being declared, after the death of two young boys hiding from police in an electricity substation. This week’s protests have shown that inequality and discrimination has not been addressed in the Paris suburbs and the mistrust between young people and police persists.

Sevran’s Lycée Blaise-Cendrars, with more than 1,000 pupils, has been at the heart of protests about school conditions before. In 2024, students and teachers made a viral video about the state of classrooms, toilets and equipment. The local Île de France region said it had put in place a major refurbishment project for high school buildings. But the teenagers said key issues had not been addressed.

“We’re starting at an unfair advantage because our parents aren’t as rich as others, they can’t buy us books, they can’t take us to films,” said Ilian, 17, whose family has Moroccan roots and whose father is a traffic warden. “We’re missing school during these protests, we risk falling behind in an exam year, we’re desperate to get back into class to study, but the conditions we’re facing are so bad we can’t stop until the government promises action.”

The education ministry this week promised 3,000 teachers to urgently fill gaps, but teachers’ unions expressed doubts and said longer-term plans and more funding was needed, even if the government argues there is little spare cash.

Children’s mental health is also an issue in Seine-Saint-Denis. Ilian has been waiting to see a child psychiatrist for months. At the high school, there was no school nurse and a lack of support staff for children with disabilities, he said.

“The police look down on us as if we’re animals”, Ilian said. “They talk to us with such cruelty.” He told local politicians that some teenagers alleged police had made racial insults against them during protests.

Stéphane Troussel, the Socialist head of the Seine-Saint-Denis département council who met the pupils this week, said: “It’s intolerable that policing is causing part of the difficulties.” He called for the police to stop using a type of rubber-bullet launcher, after they suspended use of stun grenades following injuries. The French interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, has defended policing tactics.

Stéphane Blanchet, the mayor of Sevran, said he supported the school protesters’ demands. He said many in his town of 52,000 people, with a higher than average poverty rate, felt “relegated” and forgotten by the state.

Sarah, 17, who wanted to study at an elite Paris engineering faculty, and whose warehouse worker father was proud she was protesting and meeting the mayor, said teenagers in the banlieue “really feel abandoned”.

She said: “We’ve been surprised and so appreciative of other teenagers in better-off places in France marching in the streets to support us this week. We know we’re disadvantaged and that we have to work 10 times as hard as others to escape discrimination against our postcode. But we can’t learn properly in these conditions when we’re not even guaranteed a chair to sit on in school.”
Students’ names have been changed

articles.title: Who is Jeus Yape and what is virtual taekwondo?
articles.summary: Reaping the fruits of nearly two decades spent honing his craft in taekwondo, Jeus Yape becomes the first Filipino to win a gold medal in the sport in the Asian Games

blocks.text: CHAMPION. Jeus Yape of the Philippines wins the gold medal in mixed individual virtual taekwondo in the 2026 Asian Games.
Andy Chua/Reuters
Reaping the fruits of nearly two decades spent honing his craft in taekwondo, Jeus Yape becomes the first Filipino to win a gold medal in the sport in the Asian Games

items: Jeus Yape, a 22-year-old taekwondo athlete, became the first Filipino to win a gold medal in virtual taekwondo at the Asian Games, contributing to the Philippines' total of four golds.
Yape comes from a taekwondo family and has been training in the sport since he was four years old, transitioning from kyorugi to poomsae due to his size.

His victory in virtual taekwondo has elevated him to the status of a national star, alongside established athletes Carlos Yulo and EJ Obiena, while he continues his studies in fitness and sports management.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Few knew Jeus Yape before the Asian Games.
But that changed overnight as the 22-year-old became the first Filipino to win a taekwondo gold medal in the quadrennial showpiece following his triumph in the mixed individual virtual taekwondo.

Yape helped the Philippines equal its four-gold tally in the 2018 and 2023 stagings as he delivered the last mint after Carlos Yulo claimed the floor exercise and vault titles in men’s artistic gymnastics and EJ Obiena defended his crown in men’s pole vault.
On top of his gold, Yape also bagged bronze in the men’s individual poomsae, joining Yulo as the only Filipino athletes to win multiple medals in the 20th edition held in Nagoya, Japan.
The medals are the fruits of nearly two decades Yape spent honing his craft in the sport.

Hailing from Kananga, Leyte, Yape comes from a taekwondo family, with both his father, Roderick, and mother, Joyce, holding black belts and serving as taekwondo instructors. His older sister, Stella Nicole, has also represented the country in the sport.
He first took up taekwondo at just four years old and has not looked back since.

“Back then, I just tagged along whenever my father taught classes and I spent my time playing. Eventually, he started having me join sparring sessions, and over time, I grew to like the sport,” Yape said in Filipino.
Yape started as a kyorugi (full-contact sparring) athlete before switching to poomsae (non-contact form) when he reached high school.
“I was quite small back then, so I was moved to poomsae because my size was a disadvantage in kyorugi. From then on, I became more focused on poomsae,” Yape said.

That shift paid dividends as Yape earned a taekwondo scholarship from the University of Sto. Tomas and became a member of the national team, representing the country in the 2024 World Poomsae Championships and 2025 Southeast Asian Games, where he both won bronzes as part of the mixed team.
Little did Yape know that perhaps the biggest achievement of his career would come in virtual taekwondo, an event that debuted in the Asian Games.
Yape likens virtual taekwondo or VTKD to Tekken, the popular fighting game where players aim to deplete their opponents’ health bars through a combination of attacks and strategic moves.

But instead of controllers, VTKD competitors wear virtual reality headsets to enter a digital arena, while motion-tracking nodes attached to their backs, thighs, and shins capture their movements in real time.
Attacks are measured by acceleration, with faster kicks inflicting greater damage. Competitors, though, can negate damage with successful blocks.
VTKD also borrows elements from video games, including a stun meter that renders opponents temporarily defenseless once filled. While punches do not deal damage, they help charge the stun bar.
Although VTKD requires no physical contact, Yape said the sport presents its own challenges.
“It’s difficult because you’re not hitting anything, so there’s more strain on the hamstrings since nothing absorbs the impact of your kick, especially when you kick with full force,” he said.

blocks.caption: Who is Jeus Yape and what is virtual taekwondo?

blocks.text: VTKD also demands stamina, with players delivering a steady stream of kicks in each fast-paced, one-minute round.
“I can say it’s hard because there’s luck involved. It’s anybody’s game,” Yape said.
Yape’s landmark Asian Games victory has thrust him into the same spotlight as Yulo and Obiena, two established stars he only once looked up to from afar.
For Yape, being mentioned in the same breath as the two Olympians is a tremendous honor.
“We watched kuya EJ compete in the Tokyo Olympics on TV at home. I never expected that I’d get to talk to him and be here with him,” Yape said during the heroes’ welcome for Asian Games medalists.

“I also really admire kuya Caloy. Our sport, freestyle taekwondo, has some similarities to gymnastics, so I’m really amazed by what kuya Caloy can do. He’s so good at sticking his landings and that’s one of the things I want to learn too. I’m inspired by him.”

While still riding high on his breakthrough triumph, Yape has returned to the familiar demands of student life as he continues his studies in fitness and sports management at UST’s Institute of Physical Education and Athletics.
“Things are back to normal now. I still have to catch up on the assignments and works I missed,” Yape said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Gatchalian: No 'standard practice' of leaving Senate rooms bare
articles.summary: The Office of the Ombudsman inspected the Senate office that detained Sen. Jinggoy Estrada stripped bare before handing it over to Sen. Tito Sotto, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian confirmed…

blocks.text: October 10, 2026 | 4:59pm

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman inspected the Senate office that detained Sen. Jinggoy Estrada stripped bare before handing it over to Sen. Tito Sotto, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian confirmed Saturday, October 10.
Gatchalian said the anti-graft office wrote him asking permission to inspect the room, after which a representative of the Ombudsman went to the Senate to check the facilities on Thursday, October 8.

"Wala naman silang sinabi kung ano 'yung pakay, but obviously naman 'yun, Ombudsman eh," Gatchalian said in an interview with DZMM. (They did not say what they were after, but that's obvious. It's the Ombudsman.)
Videos that spread online on Monday, October 5, the turnover deadline, showed the sixth-floor room stripped of most of its floor tiles and wall panels.

The room is reserved for the Senate president pro tempore, a post Estrada held from May 2024 to September 2025 under then-Senate President Chiz Escudero. Lacson and Sen. Loren Legarda, who later held the post, did not move in, and Estrada kept the room until he vacated it this month.
Images and clips also showed wires hanging from the walls and ceiling and electrical sockets pulled out, and what appears to be the removal of the toilet bowl, shower and pantry sink.
Gatchalian said he ordered the Senate secretary to cooperate with the Ombudsman, as the chamber does the same with the Philippine National Police and the National Bureau of Investigation.
The Office of the Sergeant-at-Arms assisted the Ombudsman's representative, who looked over the facility and the office.

Gatchalian said the Government Service Insurance System (GSIS), which owns the office as it is their building where the Senate is housed, also inspected the room a few days earlier after seeing photos of it.
The GSIS had been "concerned with the structural integrity" of the facility, Gatchalian said.
'Walang standard practice na ganoon'
Gatchalian rejected the claim of Estrada's camp that leaving a vacated office bare is standard practice in the Senate.
"Wala namang standard practice na ganoon. Ang standard practice ay pagbibigay-respeto sa isa't isa," he said. (There is no such standard practice. The standard practice is respect for one another.)
When Gatchalian moved offices in 2016, he said, then-Sen. Koko Pimentel asked whether he wanted the room as it was.
Sotto also asked whether he wanted the furniture when he vacated the Senate president's office on Friday, Gatchalian said.
Sotto ended up leaving the office as it was, down to his own chair and desk, which Gatchalian had expected him to take.
Gatchalian, whose term ends in 2028, said he would change only the work area for his staff to accommodate their larger number.
Asked if he was disappointed by Estrada's actions, Gatchalian said he was. "Nakita n'yo naman 'yung picture, bare na bare," he said. (You saw the picture. It was completely bare.)
He said Sotto would need considerable time to renovate the office and that the Senate would help in doing so.

"Sana nagkaroon ng magandang pag-uusap, sana nagkaroon ng magandang coordination para hindi made-delay 'yung paglipat ni Senator Sotto at hindi nagagastos ang gobyerno," Gatchalian said. (There should have been proper talks and coordination so Senator Sotto's move would not be delayed and the government would not have to spend money for this.)

In a statement Tuesday, Estrada's office said most of the removed items, including floor tiles, glass panels, lighting fixtures and cabinets, were bought with his personal funds because the Senate's budget for the office fell short.
It said "not a single centavo" of public funds was wasted and that the resident Commission on Audit auditor had been informed.

The statement said Estrada's chief of staff, lawyer Racquel Mejia, told Sotto's camp before the deadline that the fixtures and furnishings would be moved to Estrada's new office. It also claimed the room was already bare when Estrada received it in 2022, and called the removal of fixtures a long-standing practice in the Senate.
Sen. Ping Lacson, who turned the room over to Estrada in 2022, disputed this with publicly released videos and photos.

“I take exception to the statement pertaining to the state or condition of the same Pro Tempore office that I turned over to Sen. Estrada in 2022. Nothing was removed nor destroyed, precisely because government funds were used when I refurbished it when it was turned over to me,” Lacson said.

articles.title: When history comes to life again through a fiction novel
articles.summary: Inspired by a 1,000-year-old museum artifact, author Darwin de Jesus Mariano breathes life into the names engraved on the Laguna Copperplate with his debut fantasy novel, ‘Namwaran and the Golden…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – In the late 1990s, when the National Museum of Anthropology was still called the Museum of the Filipino People, a younger Darwin de Jesus Mariano first saw the Laguna Copperplate. It sits on a podium inside a glass case, fairly simple: a thin, hammered sheet of copper engraved with words from an ancient script.
Translated, it bears a thousand-year-old legal text recording the acquittal of a debt in gold for a man named Namwaran and his relatives.

More than two decades later, Mariano — now a Filipino author, corporate leader, tech entrepreneur, and lawyer — returned to the same museum with those names no longer confined to an inscription. He debuted his historical fantasy novel, Namwaran and the Golden Tara, on September 13, a day after its official launch at the Manila International Book Fair.

The novel is mainly inspired by the Laguna Copperplate and the Golden Tara of Agusan, following the story of three siblings: Namwaran, Angkatan, and Bukah, whose lives change after their mother disappears and the golden statue is stolen.
Mariano wove real artifacts and documented periods of Southeast Asian history into his imagination to revive the people on the copperplate.

“It all started with the scribbles on my notebook from my museum visits that fueled my fascination for ancestral history. I wondered — what if these people were on a journey and along the way, they discover the other artifacts in the Philippines and Southeast Asia?” said Mariano, explaining how he came up with the idea that bore his first novel.

Imagining these people living their lives in the past wasn’t the hard part in creating the novel. For Mariano, this was the base. It was the historical backdrop that tied it all together. The real challenge was to build an adventure out of fragments of the past.

He took the three names of relatives in the Laguna Copperplate and turned them into siblings and gave them the magic of eternal life, which they use to search for their missing mother across different eras in the novel.
“There was no mother mentioned in the artifact, so I had the freedom to create that character,” he said during the book launch.

But beneath the fiction and magic were real incidents, such as the civil wars and major eras mentioned. Specifically, Mariano lets the siblings journey through the rise and decline of regional powers such as Srivijaya and Majapahit, as well as conflicts surrounding Manila centuries later. The book also carries real historical figures from these time periods.

“I first heard about these Southeast Asian empires from an early mentor, the late senator Raul Roco. Combined with my museum notes, these learnings made me realize that the people, places, and things in our history can make for a great story,” he explained.
On the same note, Mariano said that he wants to share his appreciation for history with other Filipinos.
But Mariano had a question that followed him through years of museum visits and research: how can he make people curious about a history that can feel impossibly distant?
His answer is to create a world that is more understandable and relatable, something more familiar and easier to consume: an ancestral fantasy novel.

“We don’t have a lot of ancestral fantasy books and it’s not a common genre. Novels like this inspire curiosity and in turn, you’d want to learn more. Hopefully, this book’s readers will be interested in revisiting our history and culture,” he said.

Apart from reading historical textbooks and novels, another way to revisit the past is by going to museums. Mariano chose to hold the book launch at the National Museum of Anthropology, not just to match the theme of his novel, but also to invite the attendees to a guided tour.

The tour, guided by museum staff, featured five artifacts: the Kulaman limestone burial jars, the Maradika Qur’an, the Manunggul Jar, the Banton Burial Cloth, and finally, the Laguna Copperplate itself.
At the last stop, Mariano took over from the guide to give a short speech to explain the story of the copperplate.

“Imagine what would have been required for this document to exist in 900 AD,” he pointed out. “The society behind it would have needed systems for writing and keeping time, as well as laws, governance, and a means of recognizing when an obligation had already been settled.”
He explained that because of the contents of the copperplate, historians were able to say that this artifact is evidence of an organized society having regional connections.
However, museum pieces like this don’t fully describe the lives of those who once held them.
For National Museum of the Philippines director-general Jeremy Barns, this way of looking at the past can also change the distance Filipinos place between themselves and their ancestors.
“When we speak about our precolonial ancestors, we tend to speak about ‘them,’ when we are really talking about ‘us’,” he said in his opening remarks.

Ultimately, Mariano’s idea to fictionalize the lives of these historical characters aimed to address this issue. He created a world where these people can exist again and gave them concerns that readers could recognize: family, loss, survival, and the search for someone they love.

“We realize that they are regular people like us. They experience love, hope, fear, and sadness. In reality, they are not very different from who we are today,” he said, referring to the main characters of his novel.
During his discussion at the launch, he pointed out that there may be differences in language, place, and identity across communities, but there were also things people had in common.

For Mariano, a huge part of being interested in our history comes from the sense of connection that we have with the past. He noted that most Filipinos learn about history in school, but books, museums, and personal research made him more inclined to learn about our own culture.
He also admitted that his decade-long research and writing brought him new learnings, and that he hopes he can share these with the readers of Namwaran and the Golden Tara.
It is this sense of connection that Mariano hopes readers take with them after the adventure ends.
While Mariano’s novel aims to reconnect people with Philippine and Southeast Asian history, he admits it’s only one way to preserve our past.

The launch also came at a time when the Laguna Copperplate is being considered for inclusion in the UNESCO Memory of the World Committee for Asia and the Pacific Regional Register, a program concerned with safeguarding and widening access to documentary heritage.

During the event, UNESCO National Commission of the Philippines secretary-general Ivan Anthony Henares similarly described heritage as something that lives not only in artifacts, but also in documents, manuscripts, films, and other records.
In his remarks, he said Namwaran brings a part of the shared past “back to life, retold and made accessible to the new generation.”
For Mariano, accessibility does not have to come only from academics or cultural institutions either.
“You can be an ordinary Filipino and still be interested and spreading the word about history,” he said during the discussion.
Mariano believes Filipinos should take part in telling these stories themselves, “before other people start writing down what we should’ve been writing on our own.”
Standing once more before the artifact that had sparked his curiosity decades earlier, he left guests with another question.

“What kind of debt do we owe people like Namwaran and this family?” Mariano asked. “…the people who came before us, who lived in these islands that we now call the Philippines, that we don’t remember.”
For Mariano, remembering does not necessarily mean knowing everything about them. Much of their lives may never be recovered from the fragments that remain.
But perhaps a museum visit, a story, or an adventure can make someone curious enough to begin looking. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Mark Carney faces the return of national unity politics
articles.summary: Before this summer, it had been 30 years since a prime minister had to worry about a provincial referendum to secede. Before this week, it had been more than a decade since a prime minister was faced…

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney looks along the row of premiers at a first ministers' meeting in January. October started with a separatist party being elected into power in Quebec, and later this month Albertans will decide if they want to pursue leaving Canada. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: If it has been said that the first job of a Canadian prime minister is national unity, it was easier in recent years to forget.

Before this summer, it had been 30 years since a prime minister had to worry about a provincial referendum to secede. Before this week, it had been more than a decade since a prime minister was faced with a separatist government in Quebec.
Justin Trudeau managed to get through a full nine years as prime minister without facing either. Mark Carney is now facing both.

Speaking in the House of Commons on Tuesday, in the wake of the Parti Québécois's victory in the Quebec election, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre posited that this confluence of events could be blamed on more than a decade of Liberal government in Ottawa.

items: How anti-COVID activism injected life into Alberta's separatist movement
Alberta separatists see ally in Quebec premier-designate St-Pierre Plamondon
Before a referendum, how a new PQ government could test Ottawa

blocks.text: "Ten years ago there were no referendums in any part of the country to separate. There was no separatist movement in Alberta whatsoever, the PQ was defeated, the Bloc [Québécois] did not even have party status [in Parliament]," Poilievre said.
Correlation and causation are sometimes difficult to differentiate, but history is not quite as tidy as Poilievre remembers it.

A survey conducted in July 2014 found that 23 per cent of Albertans believed their province would be better off as its own country — equal to the share of Albertans who were recently found to be in favour of a referendum on separation.
Support for secession in Quebec was broadly unchanged by Trudeau's years in power. And the last PQ government was in office from 2012 to 2014, when Stephen Harper was prime minister.
At the time, Harper seemed disinclined to despair.

"The people of Quebec voted for change, a pretty strong desire for change," Harper said after the Quebec election in 2012. "At the same time, I think it was pretty clear they were denying any kind of a mandate to pursue the separation of Quebec or the division of the country."

In 2012, while soft-pedalling the possibility of a referendum, the Parti Québécois won 54 seats with 32 per cent of the popular vote. This week, after campaigning on an explicit commitment to hold another referendum, the PQ won 59 seats with 28 per cent of vote.
Carney could borrow Harper's 2012 analysis now — when Léger asked Quebecers in September to identify their most important issues, just nine per cent said "making Quebec a country."

The incoming premier, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, has also said a referendum won't be called while Donald Trump is president of the United States, putting off a possible vote on separation until at least 2029, before which Quebec could have another election.
But this is not an unworrisome moment for those who believe in a united Canada.
Life in a large federation

The persistence of national unity concerns across Canadian history does not necessarily speak to some inherent flaw in the federation. Some level of desire for independence might be unavoidable in a large, diverse federation — according to a poll conducted by YouGov earlier this year, for instance, 18 per cent of Americans supported their state seceding from the United States, including 27 per cent of Californians and 24 per cent of Texans.

"The standard for success in a large federation like Canada is not the absence of tensions because you see it in all large federation," says André Pratte, the journalist and former senator who chaired the Quebec Liberal Party's policy commission ahead of this year's campaign.
"But I think the success of Canada is to have been able to manage those tensions in a peaceful manner, so that we can find arrangements and pathways to solutions."
But the price of Canadian federalism might be recurring vigilance.

"In the case of Quebec, certainly, and I think probably it's the same for Alberta, there's no reason for panic," Pratte says, "but we should not be under any illusion that those things will simply go away if we just do nothing and hope that things will get better."
Carney speaks to Quebec premier-designate, says they discussed ways to 'work together'
Support in Quebec for secession is relatively low, by historical standards, but it is also still far from non-existent.

"I will never take Canada for granted," says Stéphane Dion, the former intergovernmental affairs minister who spearheaded the Clarity Act in the wake of the last Quebec referendum. "I always think we need to make the point to speak for Canada."

Pratte recalls that the sovereignists did not seem to have much chance of winning when a referendum was called in 1995, only for the end result to be a razor-thin victory for the federalist side. Referendums, once called, can quickly take on a life of their own.
What should Carney do now?

Mark Carney is well regarded in Quebec, but he would be, Pratte notes, the first non-Quebecer to contend as prime minister with a referendum in the province. There are Quebecers in prominent positions around Carney, but the government needs to be organized to react "quickly and intelligently" to developments in Quebec as they arise, Pratte says.

Speaking with CBC's Power & Politics this week, Intergovernmental Affairs Minister Dominic LeBlanc said there are a number of things on which the federal and Quebec governments can collaborate — including housing and homelessness — and that right now Quebecers "don't want governments to be hassling about some theoretical scenario in two or three years from now."

But between now and 2029, there could be various points of friction — from federal plans for high-speed rail to the monarchy. In an op-ed for the National Post this week, Pratte wrote that one challenge for the Carney government will be distinguishing between issues on which Quebec has legitimate concerns and situations where the PQ government is "merely picking a fight for tactical reasons."

On immigration, Pratte suggests, the federal government may be able to offer reasonable responses to concerns in Quebec. In his own commentary on the election result in Quebec, Dion wrote that the Carney government should show that it is a "committed ally" in promoting and protecting the French language.
At Issue | What the PQ's return means for Carney and Canada

During the Alberta referendum campaign, Carney has largely let his government's actions — namely a series of agreements with the Alberta government on energy and climate policy — speak for themselves. But when he does act, Dion says, it needs to be clear that he is not doing so simply to please or counter separatists.

"I think it must be clearer that what he has done on the pipeline and oil and energy is because he believes in it. He believes that Canada should be [an energy] superpower" Dion says. "If it's convincing some people in Alberta to believe in Canada, so be it. But it's not the main reason."

items: The Alberta question: How separatists took hold of the province’s governing party
Water, toxic waste and opportunity: Indigenous leaders react to Carney's pipeline plan

blocks.text: It remains to be seen what ramifications might follow from Alberta's referendum. And it remains to be seen whether a PQ government might require something more or different from Carney and his government.

Writing in the introduction to Straight Talk, a collection of his writing and speeches on national unity published in 1999, Dion observed that, "our typically Canadian tendency of self-deprecation has often led us to belittle our debate on unity, seeing it as only a tiresome domestic fixation, of little interest to foreigners.
"In reality, we are facing an issue that may very well be the most crucial issue of the next century: how to maintain the unity of states made up of different populations."
If that is no less true now, it only adds to the burden on every Canadian prime minister.

articles.title: Trolling or part of a larger plan?: Why Elon Musk waded into the separatism debate
articles.summary: When Elon Musk called for Quebec, Alberta and Saskatchewan to separate from Canada earlier this week, it may have been nothing more than the trillionaire engaging in some anti-Canadian trolling. But…

image.caption: Earlier this week, Elon Musk posted on X that Quebec, Alberta and Saskatchewan should separate from Canada. (ulia Demaree Nikhinson/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

When Elon Musk called for Quebec, Alberta and Saskatchewan to separate from Canada earlier this week, it may have been nothing more than the trillionaire engaging in some anti-Canadian trolling. But it's also possible 'another game' was being played.
Prime minister, premiers rejected Musk's calls for provinces to separate from Canada
When Elon Musk called for Quebec, Alberta and Saskatchewan to separate from Canada earlier this week, it may have been nothing more than the trillionaire engaging in some anti-Canadian trolling.
But it's also possible, according to one Musk observer, that the Tesla and Space X CEO had something else in mind.

"I think with Musk, there's often usually another game being played at the same time," said Quinn Slobodian, a professor of international history at Boston University who co-authored the book: Muskism: A Guide for the Perplexed.
Earlier this week, Musk took note of a post on X that stated Parti Québécois premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon had declared his dream of independence "will be realized one day."
'Would be better off'
Musk responded: "Good. Quebec should separate."
He followed up in another post: "They would be better off. Alberta and Saskatchewan should separate too."
Canadian tech journalist Paris Marx, host of the Tech Won't Save Us podcast and a regular critic of Musk, said people probably shouldn't read too much into Musk's posts.

It may be nothing more than Musk being a "right-wing troll who has a problem with countries he perceives as being more progressive or left-leaning relative to his personal politics or that he feels aggrieved by," Marx said in an email to CBC News.

items: Poilievre shrugs off Musk's pro-separatist posts: 'Canadians control their own destiny'

blocks.text: @Polymarket Good. Quebec should separate.—elonmusk

Musk's remarks were quickly rejected by Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe and Prime Minister Mark Carney. On Friday, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre also dimissed Musk's calls for separation.
'Tweets and memes do not affect Canada': Poilievre responds to Elon Musk separatism comments
Marx said Musk sees separatist movements in Canada as an opportunity to weaken the government's legitimacy.

items: Sask., Alberta premiers reject Elon Musk's call for provinces to separate from Canada

blocks.text: Yet Marx said he doesn't believe these posts were part of any calculated move on Musk's part and that Musk likely hasn't given much thought to the ramifications of the provinces separating from Canada.
Instead, Marx said the post about Quebec independence likely appeared on Musk's timeline and he simply fired off a response.
"Many people reply to posts online with knee-jerk reactions," Marx said. "Elon Musk's replies just get news articles written about them because he's incredibly rich and powerful."
Musk, the world's richest man and first-ever trillionaire, is a South African-born Canadian-American.
'Canada is not a real country'

Musk's mother Maye Musk is from Saskatchewan. Musk moved to Canada in 1989 and attended Queen's University for two years before transferring to the University of Pennsylvania. Musk's grandfather Joshua Haldeman was the leader of the Social Credit Party of Saskatchewan.
This isn't the first time Musk has weighed in on Canadian issues.

In 2025, Musk posted on X that "Canada is not a real country" following a petition calling for his passport and citizenship to be revoked over his ties to U.S. President Donald Trump. The petition received more than 375,000 signatures.

Musk also commented on Canadian politics earlier last year when he criticized then-prime minister Justin Trudeau, referring to him as an "insufferable tool." Meanwhile, he praised and endorsed Poilievre.
Carney responds to Elon Musk's support for Quebec sovereignty
Slobodian said Musk has a reflexive dislike of Canada and what he perceives as its excessively progressive policies.
So when it come to separatism, "it's like any enemy of Ottawa is a friend of mine," Slobodian said.

But Musk has also shown a keen interest in political movements abroad, particularly in Europe. For example, he has been vocal in his supprt of the far-right, anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.

A Feb. 2025 NBC News report said Musk had been encouraging right-wing political movements, policies and administrations in at least 18 countries as part of a global push to slash immigration and curtail regulation of business.
Connection with far-right politics
Slobodian said he believes there is a connection between Musk's recent comments on separatism and his affiliation with far-right politics in Europe.
With legacy parties across the European continent facing disruption from agile newcomers, Slobodian said Musk has a "pretty reasonable strategy" to create a bonds or affiliations with them.
"Then when they are the ruling parties, you've got an automatic buy-in or partner," Slobodian said.
He said Musk sees the EU and Canada in their present forms as obstacles to his accumulation strategy, and that any disruption could open new opportunities for him and his products.

"I think his idea is to jump on the secessionist train early, and if it does come to pass, then he's got kind of [a competitive] advantage," Slobodian said. "And if it doesn't, then so what? It just fades off into the background again."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Mark Gollom is a Toronto-based reporter with CBC News. He covers Canadian and U.S. politics and current affairs.
With files from Peter Zimonjic

articles.title: AI photos are making it harder to know what you're booking on Airbnb. Here's what to look out for
articles.summary: Josh Wells was excited to explore Montreal on his first trip outside the U.S. But as he scrolled through listings on Airbnb, he noticed something odd: Several host profile pictures and one listing…

image.caption: Josh Wells noticed that text on an artwork in an Airbnb listing looked jumbled, which raised his suspicions that the image had been edited or generated using AI. (Josh Wells/Reddit)

blocks.text: LISTEN | When Airbnb photos don't match reality:
Cost of Living5:19Can you believe what you see on Airbnb?

Josh Wells, a college student from Iowa, was excited to explore Montreal on his first trip outside the U.S. But as he scrolled through Airbnb listings in search of a place to stay, he began to notice something that didn't seem quite right.
Several of the hosts renting out their properties had profile pictures that Wells suspected were generated by artificial intelligence.
"Your average person taking an iPhone photo, there's obviously like a little bit of imperfections," Wells told the CBC's Cost of Living. "The AI photos, they just looked too perfect."
Still, Wells kept browsing. He was even close to booking one of the properties when a final look at the listing's photos raised another red flag.

He zoomed in on a piece of wall art depicting two halves of faces joined together. At the top, the artwork appeared to read "Picasso." But in another photo of the same room, taken from a different angle, the artwork looked different.
"The text was all warped and funky," he said. "I'm just like, 'Yeah, OK, this is AI."

When booking his trip to Montreal, Wells found extremely polished-looking photos of hosts appeared in numerous Airbnb listings, leading him to suspect they had been generated using AI. Short-term rentals in that city are subject to strict rules aimed in part at protecting the city's housing supply. (Josh Wells/Reddit)

That was enough to put Wells off the listing — and ultimately using Airbnb for this trip. Unable to tell whether the photos showed a real place or an AI-generated version of one, he opted for an apartment-style hotel instead.
"The fake profile picture is one thing, but listings of the actual place that you're staying at and spending thousands of dollars was an immediate no for me," Wells said.
Wells isn't the only traveller to question whether the photos found on Airbnb or similar short-term rental-style platforms accurately reflect reality.

items: Why some travellers are falling out of love with Airbnb

blocks.text: In July, an Ottawa family reported that their daughter arrived at a Toronto Airbnb to find a room that looked significantly different from the listing photos, which they suspected had been generated or heavily altered using AI.

The family provided side-by-side photos showing differences in the room and bathroom. Airbnb said the listing did not match the property and refunded the guest, but did not confirm whether artificial intelligence had been used.

As AI makes it easier to alter photos, experts say travellers may find it increasingly difficult to know whether Airbnb-style listings accurately reflect reality, raising questions about consumer trust and protections in Canada.
When a photo makeover goes too far

The proliferation of free, quick and easy-to-use AI tools is making photo editing increasingly tempting, said Francis Syms, associate dean in the faculty of applied sciences and technology at Humber Polytechnic in Toronto.

Beyond the major AI platforms, such as ChatGPT, Claude by Anthropic and Google's Gemini, countless other websites offer free tools for modifying images, said Syms. Hugging Face, for example, hosts thousands of AI tools that let users upload and edit photos.

"In a matter of 10 seconds, you can upload a picture to one of these sites and ask it to remove all the smudges or to change the furniture," he said. "You'll get that image back maybe 30 to 60 seconds later."
Artificial intelligence platforms like ChatGPT allows users to quickly and easily edit photos. (Marco Bertorello/AFP via Getty Images)
It's difficult to know where AI editing crosses into deception, said Daniel Guttentag, an associate professor of hospitality and tourism management at the College of Charleston in South Carolina.

"If you put in a fake hot tub on the back patio, I think basically everyone would agree that that is a blatant misrepresentation of what one's unit offers," he said. "Whereas if you just start to play with the lighting a little bit … I think most people would be comfortable with that.
"But then there's a whole lot of space in between, when it crosses that line into, 'Wait, this isn't what I signed up for.'"
Guttentag said another concern is the use of AI-edited images to make it appear that guests have damaged a property, potentially leading to compensation claims.
In 2025, a guest from London, U.K., booked an Airbnb in Manhattan and was accused of causing more than £12,000 ($22, 665) in damage.
She disputed the claim after noticing inconsistencies in photos of a supposedly cracked coffee table, which she suspected had been digitally manipulated or generated by AI.
Airbnb initially said she owed more than £5,000 ($9,444), but later fully refunded her after the case drew media attention.
Can you trust what you see online?
Relying on listing photos to decide which property to book makes trust particularly important for Airbnb guests, said Guttentag.
"You can't try it on in advance, like a pair of shoes," he said. "You have to have the confidence and the trust that it's going to live up to your expectations."

Although AI-altered photos might help hosts attract bookings in the short term, guests who arrive to find something different than what was advertised may leave negative reviews, Guttentag said. If people feel misled "one too many times," he said, it could prompt them to stop using the platform altogether.

Daniel Guttentag is an associate professor of hospitality and tourism management at the College of Charleston in South Carolina with research interests in Airbnb and artificial intelligence. (Submitted by Daniel Guttentag)

In a statement to CBC News, Airbnb says its rules require listings to be "accurately represented" and that the company may ask hosts to remove content that uses AI or other digital technology to "edit flaws, hide damage, add amenities or attributes that are not part of a listing, or otherwise materially misrepresent the listing."

The company further said it encourages guests to report misleading listings and that those who find a property that doesn't match its description can contact its 24/7 community support team. Under AirCover, Airbnb added, it may help guests find a similar place or provide a refund if the host can't resolve the issue.

In August, California's Artificial Intelligence Transparency Act (CAITA) took effect, requiring AI-generated images, videos and audio to carry information that can help consumers identify whether digital content was created or altered using AI.

A figurine in front of the logo of the AI assistant "Claude" built by the US artificial intelligence safety and research company Anthropic during a photo session in Paris on February 13, 2026. (Joel Saget/AFP via Getty Images)

Canada doesn't yet have AI-specific legislation addressing misleading advertising, said Steve Szentesi, a Toronto-based competition and advertising lawyer. But he said existing laws can already apply to deceptive AI-generated images.

The federal Competition Act prohibits misleading advertising, whether the claims are made through text, photos, audio or other forms of media. Provincial and territorial consumer protection laws offer similar safeguards.

While AI-generated images are relatively novel, the underlying issue is not, Szentesi said. Courts have dealt with disputes over real estate listings for decades, including cases where photos of a property didn’t match the home itself or contradicted descriptions in the listing.

For consumers who believe a short-term rental listing misrepresents a property, Szentesi suggests first raising it with the rental platform. They can also file a complaint with the Competition Bureau or their provincial or territorial consumer protection act.

items: AI 'slop' is dominating menus, as some restaurant owners turn to it to save time and money
Can I get AI face? Plastic surgeons say AI-generated inspiration is more than meets the eye

blocks.text: In the meantime, Syms suggests would-be bookers look for possible signs of AI-generated images in listing photos, such as crooked door frames, tile lines and countertops, oddly shaped furniture, inconsistent shadows or reflections, and blurry or jumbled words on books or wall art.
Travellers can also use a tool like Google Lens, he said, to search for the same image online and check whether it has been taken from another website rather than showing the actual property.

For Wells, the experience hasn't ruled out him using Airbnb altogether — he had a positive experience booking with the platform in Kansas City in March. But his search for a place in Montreal has made him more wary, he said.
"I am open to it again as long as there's just no fake AI listings involved."

articles.title: He was ready to fight in the 'war on terror.' This post-9/11 veteran looks back at his decision to enlist
articles.summary: After the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, CBC’s chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault reported on young people who enlisted to fight in the global "war on terror." Twenty-four years later, she tracked down…

blocks.text: He went to war after 9/11. It changed him forever
On Sept. 11, 2001, Barry Sward, a high school senior in Woodbridge, Va., watched the collapse of the twin towers on TV and knew he had made the right decision.
He had already enlisted to become a U.S. marine. Emboldened by a national tragedy, he now had an enemy to fight.

"There was a spike of revenge … and I did want to get the people that did this and hurt them really bad. I don't know why they're doing it," he told CBC News chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault, who at the time was reporting on post-9/11 military recruitment.

In July 2002, he would start basic training at Parris Island, S.C., and just months later was part of the first units to enter Iraq as part of U.S. President George W. Bush's so-called "war on terror."

After Sept. 11, 2001, U.S. veterans are about twice as likely as those who signed up before them to have served in a combat zone, according to a 2019 Pew Research survey that polled 1,284 veterans. As a result, they are more likely to have been scarred by the battle wounds of war — not only physically, but mentally, too.
In that same survey, half of the respondents said they had emotionally traumatic or distressing experiences, yet only a third sought help to deal with what they faced.

CBC News chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault, left, sits with U.S. marine vetreran Barry Sward, who shares photos and mementoes he saved from his time serving in Iraq in 2003, including a half pack of cigarettes, cassettes and his service cap. (Roxanna Woloshyn/CBC News)
In August of this year, Arsenault tracked down an almost unrecognizable Sward in Falmouth, Va., 24 years after their first interview.
She asked him: "Are you the same person you were when you went in?"
"No, definitely not," said Sward, now facing the effects of that deployment to Iraq — a resulting back injury and a PTSD diagnosis.
The post-9/11 patriotic recruits
In the days and months after the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, media reports described long lines at military recruitment offices made up of young people who wanted to fight for their country.

"Post-9/11, you have a burst of patriotism and a need to serve, and there are plenty of stories of people who immediately left their jobs, went down to a recruiting station, or finally decided that they were gonna join," said Jason Dempsey, a scholar of American civil military relations at Columbia University.
"But that was not the majority of folks entering service. And in the grand scheme of things was a very temporary blip."
Sward, seen here in 2002, participated in basic training at Parris Island, S.C., as part of his preparations in the U.S. marine corps beginning in July 2002. (CBC News)
Numbers provided by the four primary branches of the military don't show a dramatic rise in enlistment immediately following Sept. 11 compared to other years.

Dempsey said the most common reasons for someone to join the military is a history of service in their families, a desire for financial security or educational opportunities and enlisting during a period of high unemployment.

Regardless of their reason for signing up, that generation of post-9/11 fighters would go on to participate in long-lasting wars in Afghanistan and Iraq — the latter of which saw U.S. foces officially withdraw just last month.
Serving in Iraq was 'frustrating'
In March 2003, as part of the global war on terror, U.S. President Bush announced forces would be invading Iraq if then-president Saddam Hussein did not leave.

Days later, Sward's unit, the 2nd Battalion, 8th Marines, crossed into the country. Their mission was to secure bridges in a highly defended enemy territory so troops could ultimately make their way to Baghdad.
March 23, 2003, is a day that haunts Sward. It was the beginning of a deadly fight known as the Battle of Nasiriyah.
Eighteen of his fellow marines died, including a friend he met in basic training.

"It was tough. There was a lot of screaming, obviously, and we could hear it happening," said Sward. "And that was the frustrating part — knowing that something else was going on, not too far away from you, but can't do anything about it."

U.S. marines from Task Force Tarawa duck as a helicopter fires a missile that destroys a building during a deadly gun battle on March 23, 2003, in the southern Iraqi city of Nasiriyah. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)
While there, his unit was tasked with patrolling inside the city and looking for leadership and evidence of weapons of mass destruction.

Bush rationalized the invasion of Iraq on unverified U.S. intelligence that the country's leadership was harbouring destructive devices that would cause massive damage to populations if deployed. In the years since, no evidence was ever found that those weapons existed.
During the interview in August, Arsenault asked Sward what it was like knowing this in hindsight.
"It's frustrating. Still proud to have served, but maybe there were some political aspects that were at play in the background," said Sward.

More than 7,000 troops died in post-9/11 wars, according to research from Brown University's Costs of War project, and four times as many U.S. military personnel have died by suicide in the years since.
Since then, those wars have been looked at with a critical eye as to whether they accomplished what they set out to do.
That same Pew Research survey found that 64 per cent of veterans say the war in Iraq was not worthwhile, and similarly, 58 per cent said the same about Afghanistan.
Post-9/11 vets made progress addressing PTSD

Sward's time serving in Iraq was cut short. He suffered chronic back pain due to a spinal issue, and he returned to the base in Camp Lejeune, N.C., that same year, and was eventually processed out of the marine corps.
But it would take 14 years for Sward to get a diagnosis for the deeper pain he was struggling with: PTSD.

"Mine tends to show up as anger. I was either sad or I was pissed off and there wasn't any in-between. It took me a lot of therapy and I learned a lot from my wife," said Sward. His wife, Rebecca, is a licensed psychotherapist.
"I was either going to get help or I was going to lose my wife and my wonderful kids. I definitely made the right choice."
"As he's gotten older, I think he's been more open to unpacking trauma and trying to heal," said Rebecca, whom he met after he returned home. They’ve been married 21 years and have four children.
Sward poses with his wife, Rebecca, right, and four children. (Roxanna Woloshyn/CBC News)

According to the U.S. Department of Veteran Affairs, 29 per cent of veterans who served in Iraq or Afghanistan will have had PTSD at some point in life, compared to 10 per cent who served in Vietnam and three per cent who served in the Second World War and the Korean War.

"Back in those times, I don't think the rates were really lower if we look at actual cases, but I think a lot of people could not come forward. They couldn't say that they were still struggling with nightmares or with flashbacks or other reminders of the war," said Timothy Hoyt, chief mental health officer with the U.S. Defence Health Agency in Falls Church, Va.
"We've seen a lot of progress in addressing those stigma concerns in the last 20 years."
Despite the trauma he faced, Sward says he still takes great pride in the time he served in the marines, he just won't encourage his children to sign up.
"I have no regrets. All my choices have led me here to this moment where I have my beautiful wife and four kids."

articles.title: CALABARZON minimum wage earners get up to P45 daily raise
articles.summary: Minimum wage earners in CALABARZON will get up to P45 more a day starting October 26, the region’s wage board announced Saturday, October 10.

blocks.text: October 10, 2026 | 3:30pm

Activists Kilusang Mayo Uno (KMU) staged a protest rally in front of the House of Representative to call for the lawmaker to pass the national minimum wage bill would increase workers wages to 750 pesos nationwide.
Boy Santos, file
MANILA, Philippines — Minimum wage earners in CALABARZON will get up to P45 more a day starting October 26, the region’s wage board announced Saturday, October 10.
The raise, worth as much as P1,170 a month, will cover more than 1.56 million minimum wage earners across the region, according to the National Wages and Productivity Commission.
Not every worker will get the full P45 as the increase depends on the worker’s industry and on how the city or town where they work is classified, based on Wage Order No. IVA-23.
The Regional Tripartite Wages and Productivity Board 4A did not include that breakdown in its announcement. It said the rates per sector and area are listed in the official copy of the order.

The regional board and the NWPC, both made up of labor, employer and government representatives, approved the rates after reviewing the region’s economic and social conditions, as required by Republic Act 6727 or the Wage Rationalization Act.
Labor Secretary Francis Tolentino, who chairs the commission, led the meeting that set the new rates.
Tolentino said the Department of Labor and Employment’s CALABARZON office will closely monitor establishments to make sure they comply.
The new order follows Wage Order No. IVA-22, which raised daily pay in the region by P25 to P100 in two tranches, on Oct. 5, 2025 and April 1 this year.
Daily minimum wages in CALABARZON currently range from P508 to P600, depending on the sector and the municipality’s classification.
Prices at three-year high
The raise comes as inflation rose to 7.2% in September from 6.1% in August, matching April’s rate and the fastest since March 2023, the Philippine Statistics Authority reported.
Rice inflation climbed to a high 20.3%, and inflation among the poorest 30% of households reached 9%.

articles.title: NBI invites Pulong Duterte to 'shed light' on Gracioso claims
articles.summary: The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) on Saturday said it invited Davao City Representative Paolo "Pulong" Duterte to provide his insights on the claims of dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso.

blocks.text: Published October 10, 2026 3:11pm
The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) on Saturday said it invited Davao City Representative Paolo "Pulong" Duterte to provide his insights on the claims of dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso.

"The Bureau expressed its compliments to the lawmaker and requested his presence to shed light on the circumstances surrounding the inquiry. The NBI emphasized that Rep. Duterte's insights would significantly support the agency in ensuring a fair, thorough, and impartial process," the bureau said in a media advisory.

Gracioso had earlier accused the Davao congressman, his sister Vice President Sara Duterte, and their father, former president Rodrigo Duterte, of accepting bags of cash from former House speaker Lord Allan Velasco.
The NBI said Paolo Duterte was sent an invitation from NBI Director Melvin Matibag in a letter dated October 5. Duterte was also sent a copy of Gracioso's sworn affidavit.
The NBI set the meeting with the lawmaker on October 12, at its own headquarters.

"The Bureau noted that Rep. Duterte may be accompanied by legal counsel or designated representatives. He is also invited to present relevant documents, records, or statements that may assist in clarifying the issues under review," the NBI said.
GMA News Online has reached out to Paolo Duterte office regarding the matter, but he has yet to respond as of posting time.
The vice president has already denied Gracioso's claims, saying he was only making the claims for money and because of resentment towards Velasco and his family.
Her office is set to submit her own affidavit to contradict Gracioso's claim.

Velasco's camp earlier called out "fabricated attacks" against him, saying these have "no basis." It also called out accusations against Velasco as "inconsistent," tailored as a "one-size fits all" narration.
The Bureau of Immigration (BI) confirmed Tuesday that Velasco is out the country, saying he does not have a derogatory record that would prevent his departure. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Recruitment boss accused of being behind ‘doxxing’ campaign against RNLI and anti-racism activists
articles.summary:
Tom Watson, of Worcester, alleged to be behind Big Time Charlie X account that created so-called Traitorbase

The owner of a recruitment firm has been accused of being at the centre of a…

blocks.text: The owner of a recruitment firm has been accused of being at the centre of a so-called “doxxing” campaign against the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI), anti-racism activists and business executives who recruit black, Asian and minority ethnic workers.
Tom Watson, from Worcester, is alleged to be behind an X account calling itself “Big Time Charlie”, which was deactivated shortly after he was named by the campaign group Hope Not Hate.

The account had almost 50,000 followers and had become increasingly prominent in recent weeks as RNLI staff found themselves being harassed and attacked online as far-right activists targeted them over their involvement in rescuing people trying to cross the Channel in small boats.

The account, which has a history of racist comments, appears to have been using AI to scrape data from LinkedIn and other sites to build a so-called Traitorbase. The Big Time Charlie account was removed almost immediately after Hope Not Hate alleged that Watson was behind it, and after the Guardian approached him for comment.

Like the posts on Watson’s LinkedIn account, the X account has frequently praised the hard-right MP Rupert Lowe. It also claimed to have donated £2,500 to Lowe’s Restore Britain party and joined its “Cromwell Club” for those activists who pay a certain level of donation.
Targets of doxxing by the Big Time Charlie account told the Guardian of the impact.

They included Chantelle Lunt, a Green party councillor in Merseyside who has already been targeted by the far right, and who made a report to the police after details about her were published online by the account.

She said: “Someone told me that I had been doxxed and when I went to look I saw that details about me appeared to be on a spreadsheet which included reference to other people who were involved in Stand Up to Racism.

“The climate at the moment is horrendous and I’m no stranger to people targeting me and my family, but there’s a big concern when this information is actively put out there. You can see people engaging with it and actively encouraging each other.”

A spokesperson for a charity that was targeted told the Guardian: “This is another example of a cynical attempt to spread misinformation that has unfortunately gone unchecked on social media platforms.
“This is an attempt to sow discord and division among communities and prevent organisations trying to help the most vulnerable communities in this country from operating at their full potential.

“Time spent combating misinformation and bigotry is a distraction from these organisations’ programme work here at home, which actually makes a difference in the ordinary lives of people in the UK. Social media companies, the media and politicians have a responsibility to clamp down on misinformation and the division it causes.”
A number of businesses, big and small, were also doxxed on the account, which posted the photographs and names of executives who were said to have been involved in hiring minority ethnic staff.
A businessperson who was also targeted described their doxxing by the account as “bizarre”.

“Thankfully it doesn’t seem to have led to any problems, but it’s not something that you expect to have to contend with. It’s a pretty unpleasant thing to do, especially if it’s someone who is involved in their own business,” they added.

Watson divides his time between the UK and US and founded the recruitment firm Futura Energy Group, which describes itself as “a specialist recruitment and build-with talent partner for companies operating across AI”.
Archived online records show that the Big Time Charlie account originally bore the name Tom Watson, while a range of other evidence links him to it.
That included regular references by the account to being in Puerto Rico, where Futura is based according to its LinkedIn account, and references to working in recruitment for technical roles.

The Big Time Charlie account posted on 20 July that they were in Zurich and shared a photo taken in the grounds of the Vitznauerhof hotel. Two days later, Watson posted on his LinkedIn profile that he was in Switzerland and shared another image taken from the Vitznauerhof hotel.
Watson was approached for comment.

articles.title: ‘Chiz with his cheese’: Squishy hype reaches Senate impeachment trial
articles.summary: Escudero has been spotted fiddling with a squishy toy during the impeachment trial

blocks.text: STRESS-RELIEVER. Senate Impeachment court presiding officer Chiz Escudero holds a squishy toy during the trial.
RAPPLER SCREENGRAB
Escudero has been spotted fiddling with a squishy toy during the impeachment trial
Participating in an impeachment trial is stressful, but presiding over one? A totally different story.
Senate Impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero appears to have found a way to manage courtroom pressure of overseeing the proceedings: a bright yellow, cheese-shaped squishy toy.

Much to its name, squishies are soft, squeezable toys designed to slowly return to their original shape after being compressed. They come in various shapes, sizes, and textures, with some offering a crunchy or resistant feel. The toys have been trending on social media, with some content creators making hauls or autonomous sensory meridian response (ASMR) videos.

During the impeachment trial, Escudero was repeatedly seen fiddling with a bright yellow, rectangular squishy resembling a cheese. At one point, he even delivered a ruling on a prosecution slide that had briefly appeared on the screen while playing with his squishy.
“Can the clerk kindly check with the tech what was flashed and upon whose authority it was flashed,” Escudero said.
Squishies may be marketed as toys for children, but they can also be great stress-relievers for adults.
And with Escudero celebrating his birthday on Saturday, October 10, a great gift idea, perhaps, could be another squishy! – Rappler.com

articles.title: Palace rejects Mans Carpio's 'collateral damage' claim, joins his 'prayer for truth'
articles.summary: Malacañang rejected on Saturday Second Gentleman Atty. Mans Carpio"s remark that he is collateral damage in his wife Vice President Sara"s impeachment trial, and stated that it will join Carpio to…

blocks.text: Published October 10, 2026 2:32pm

Malacañang rejected on Saturday Second Gentleman Atty. Mans Carpio’s remark that he is collateral damage in his wife Vice President Sara’s impeachment trial, and stated that it will join Carpio to pray “for the truth.”

“Well, tulungan natin magdasal si Mans Carpio. 'Yan ang gusto nating lahat ng Pilipino — magdasal para lumabas ang katotohanan kasi maraming nabubulag ngayon,” Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said.
(Well, let’s help Mans Carpio pray. That is what all Filipinos want—to pray for the truth to come out because many are being blinded right now.)
Speaking at an event on Thursday, Carpio said that they are praying that the issues surrounding him and his wife will finally come to an end.
“Nagdarasal na lang kami na sana matapos na (We are just praying that it will end soon), God willing,” Carpio said.
Castro said they will join Carpio in his prayer, emphasizing turning to the true God.
“Pero kung magdasal tayo, dapat sa totoong Diyos. Hindi kung sinong diyos-diyosan diyan,” Castro said.
(But if we pray, it should be to the true God—not to just any false idol out there.)
Carpio also accused the government of using everything against them and dragging him into the issue as if he were the one being impeached and becoming collateral damage.
“Wala sila makita kay Sara kaya parang collateral damage ako,” the Second Gentleman alleged.
(They can’t find anything on Sara, so it seems like I’m collateral damage.)
For its part, the Palace said that the people deserved full transparency regarding all the evidence available, citing the President’s previous statement that no one will be singled out.

“Dahil sa panahon ni Pangulo Marcos Jr., hindi ginagawa ang pag-cover-up. walang sinisino. Sabi nga natin, kamag-anak, kaibigan, kaalyado, kung may makikitang ebidensya laban sa kanila patungkol sa anomalya, dapat itong imbestigahan,” Castro said.

(Because under President Marcos Jr., cover-ups are not allowed. No one is spared. As we have said, whether relative, friend, or ally, if evidence of wrongdoing is found against them, it must be investigated.)
“So kung may nadadamay lamang, sinasabi nila, malamang ay may ebidensya so kung wala namang ebidensya malilinis naman nila ang kanila mga pangalan,” she added.
(So if someone is being dragged into this, as they claim, it is likely because there is evidence. If there is no evidence, they will be able to clear their names.)

On Day 37 of the Vice President’s impeachment trial, a prosecution witness testified that Duterte and her husband were found to have unexplained wealth and undeclared assets amounting to P817.87 million. —KG, GMA News
