articles.title: 'Stain on the country': Trump criticises Norway over Nobel Peace Prize
articles.summary: The US president told a rally he had "never heard of" the winner, former International Criminal Court judge Navi Pillay.

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump has once again made complaints that he did not receive the Nobel Peace Prize, calling this year's decision "disgraceful and embarrassing".
The prize was awarded to former International Criminal Court judge Navi Pillay on Friday. Hours after the announcement, Donald Trump told a rally he had "never heard" of the "mystery person".
"This is an indelible stain on the country of Norway" he said, adding "we will not forget".
Trump has been outspoken about his desire to win the prize, and made similar criticisms in 2025 when it was awarded to Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado.
Last year, Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre explained to Trump it was an independent committee based in Norway, not the Norwegian government, which decides who will receive the prize.
Speaking to his supporters at a rally in Syracuse, New York, the US president repeated claims that he had settled eight wars and was "about to settle or win two more", without providing evidence.
"The Nobel Peace Prize has been forever discredited by a handful of radical ideologues who are anti-democracy and really enemies of civilisation," he said.

Pillay, a former UN human rights chief and International Court of Justice judge, was recognised "for her efforts to promote peace and international law", which paved the way for a "more comprehensive global legal order", the Nobel committee said.

The South African's work had been "instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide are prosecuted", said the chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee Jørgen Watne Frydnes.
Shortly afterwards, the 85-year-old reacted to the news from Nuremberg's Palace of Justice by saying "it must be a joke" and thanked those who had gathered to applaud her.
"If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," she joked.
Last year, the president openly expressed his displeasure at missing out on the prize, with the White House accusing the committee of placing "politics over peace".
In January, Machado gifted her medal to Trump during a meeting at the White House, which she said was in recognition of his commitment to her country's freedom.
Trump said on social media that the move was "a wonderful gesture of mutual respect".
The Nobel committee later clarified that the prize was not transferable.
"Once a Nobel Prize is announced, it cannot be revoked, shared, or transferred to others," it said in a statement. "The decision is final and stands for all time."

blocks.text: Published October 10, 2026 11:52am
Malacañang has accepted the resignation of Secretary Henry Aguda of the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT), Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla said Saturday.

Remulla made the announcement when he was asked on his radio program about the fate of Aguda, who had admitted in a statement read during a recent Palace briefing that he was "aware of reports circulating" regarding his position.
"Nag-resign. Tinanggap na 'yung resignation," Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla said in his radio program.
(He resigned. His resignation was accepted.)
GMA News Online has reached out to Aguda, Malacañang, and the DICT for comment on the matter, but they have yet to respond as of posting time.

The development comes just three days after Press Press Officer Undersecretary Atty. Claire Castro said Aguda would stay on as the agency's chief. At the time, she said the Palace has not received information about Aguda's resignation.
Aguda assumed the helm at the DICT in March 2025, succeeding Ivan Uy.

In his statement read by Castro, Aguda said, "As Secretary of DICT, I serve at the pleasure of the President, and I fully recognize and respect the President’s prerogative in matters concerning his Cabinet and his administration. My focus remains on carrying out my responsibilities and serving the Filipino people to the best of my ability." — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: ICC allows seven more drug war incidents in Duterte case
articles.summary: The International Criminal Court has allowed prosecutors to add seven killings to the crimes against humanity case against former President Rodrigo Duterte, but struck out an eighth because it fell…

blocks.text: October 10, 2026 | 11:39am

MANILA, Philippines — The International Criminal Court has allowed prosecutors to add seven more incidents to the crimes against humanity case against former President Rodrigo Duterte, but struck out an eighth because it fell outside the time period of the charge it was filed under.

In the same October 9 decision, the ICC Trial Chamber III also rejected a defense request to order the prosecutors to rewrite the charges against Duterte as a closed list of killings. Duterte’s lawyers had argued that because the prosecutors treat the listed incidents as examples, he cannot know which specific incidents he will have to answer for at his trial, which opens November 30.

The ruling brings the Duterte case's incident count to 56. The 49 incidents confirmed by the Pre-Trial Chamber in April charge Duterte with 76 murders and two attempted murders. The public version of this latest decision does not say how many murders or attempted murders are in the seven new incidents.
Police reported at least 6,252 deaths in anti-drug operations during Duterte's presidency, but rights groups estimate the true number is up to 30,000, including vigilante-style killings.
The charges
Duterte faces three counts, or separate charges, of murder as a crime against humanity.

Prosecutors must prove each count on its own and the judges are expected to rule on each separately, so Duterte could be convicted on one and acquitted on another. The counts are divided by time period and by type of killing.

items: Count 1 covers killings in Davao City from 2013 to around June 2016, while Duterte was mayor. Prosecutors attribute these killings to the Davao Death Squad, which it accuses Duterte of having ultimate command over. This count lists 19 people killed in Incidents 1 to 9.
Count 2 covers killings of "high-value targets," or alleged major drug figures, from July 2016 to July 2017, Duterte's first year as president. The count lists 14 people killed in Incidents 10 to 14.

Count 3 covers killings of low-level suspects in police raids to clear barangays of drugs as part of "Oplan Tokhang," from July 2016 to September 2018. It lists 43 people killed and two who survived in Incidents 15 to 49, and is the only count that also charges attempted murder.

blocks.text: The eight new incidents
Prosecutors gave notice of Incidents 50 to 57 on August 31, the deadline the chamber set in May, and detailed them in their trial brief filed September 4.

On September 11, the defense asked the ICC judges to strike them or make prosecutors seek the Pre-Trial Chamber's approval, arguing that all eight involved new locations, victims, perpetrators and dates.

The chamber admitted Incidents 50 to 55 under Count 3 and Incident 56 under Count 2. It found that each falls within its count's time period and within the charges' scope of "locations across the Philippines."
However, the judges decided to reject Incident 57, filed under Count 2, because it falls outside the July 2016 to July 2017 period that Count 2 covers.

Witnesses for the new incidents are not expected to testify in the first months of the trial, and the chamber told both sides to ensure none is called before the defense has had reasonable time to prepare.
Request to refile charges rejected

Lead defense counsel Peter Haynes argued in an August 31 motion that charges built on "illustrative" and "non-exhaustive" incidents violate Duterte's right under the Rome Statute to be told in detail what he is charged with. He called the charges a "moving target" and asked the chamber to order prosecutors to refile them before the Pre-Trial Chamber with a complete list of acts.
However, in its decision, the chamber's judges said they have no power to do that as only the prosecutor can seek to change confirmed charges, and only with the Pre-Trial Chamber's permission.

Trial chambers cannot review pre-trial decisions on appeal and the motion re-argued issues Pre-Trial Chamber I had already settled, including when it refused the defense permission to appeal on May 21, the decision read.

The judges also rejected the argument that prosecutors need pre-trial approval for each new incident. The charges were confirmed as covering "at least" the named victims, and the pre-trial judges had called incident-by-incident approval "practically unworkable."
The chamber found that the confirmed charges, the confirmation proceedings and the trial brief give Duterte enough detail to prepare his defense.
Why the exact number of incidents matter

To convict, prosecutors must prove beyond reasonable doubt that the killings happened, that they were part of a widespread or systematic attack on civilians under a state or organizational policy, and that Duterte is responsible for them.
Each incident names a date, place, victim and alleged perpetrators that the defense must prepare to answer during the trial.
What's next
Prosecutors must file their revised trial brief, witness list and evidence list by October 16. The defense must file its list of contested issues by October 30.
Duterte has been ruled fit to stand trial.

articles.title: Hurricane Isaias makes landfall on U.S. Gulf Coast as Category 2 storm
articles.summary: Hurricane Isaias crashed into the U.S. Gulf Coast as a dangerous Category 2 storm on Friday, lashing communities in Alabama and the Florida Panhandle with damaging winds, heavy rain, flooding and…

image.caption: An American flag is seen flapping in the wind on Alabama's Mon Louis Island ahead of the arrival of Hurricane Isaias on Friday. (Octavio Jones/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·Updated

Hurricane Isaias crashed into the U.S. Gulf Coast as a dangerous Category 2 storm on Friday, lashing communities in Alabama and the Florida Panhandle with damaging winds, heavy rain, flooding and life-threatening storm surge.
U.S. National Hurricane Center says Isaias made landfall near Destin, Fla., on Friday

The first hurricane of the Atlantic season made landfall near Destin, Fla., the Miami-based U.S. National Hurricane Center said. It had maximum sustained winds of 169 km/h. The storm weakened to just below major hurricane status before it came ashore.

"The storm is here. Buckle down at this point. Don't be getting out on the roads," Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said at a news conference, adding that flash flooding would be a hazard "throughout the region."

Hurricane-force winds lashed the Gulf shoreline in the low-lying coastal area known for powdery white sand beaches that are dotted with vacation homes, waterfront bars and seafood shacks. Forecasters warned the conditions could also stir up tornadoes.
People are seen leaving a gas station in Mobile, Ala., on Friday, which had been boarded up prior to the hurricane's arrival. (Octavio Jones/The Associated Press)
In Mobile, Ala., officials reported downed trees and power lines, while Emerald Coast Utilities Authority, which serves parts of Florida, issued a boil-water notice for its customers.
More than 400,000 customers in Florida and Alabama were without power Friday evening, according to poweroutage.com.
Residents in Panama City, Fla., braved the rain while filling sandbags Friday to protect their houses.
"I mean, it's just the nature of the beast. It's Florida," said Corliss Stone, who works for the fire department.
A downed tree blocks a road in Pensacola, Fla., on Friday, as Isaias-driven wind and rain approached the area. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

One of the biggest concerns is a storm surge that could be as high as 1.8 to 2.7 metres, according to the hurricane centre. Places most at risk include Florida's Pensacola Beach and the Gulf Islands National Seashore.

Anne Petzold, who lives with her husband in the Florida beach community of Gulf Breeze, said everyone in their neighbourhood planned to ride out the storm. The couple installed hurricane shutters and picked up anything in their yard that could turn into a projectile.
"Everybody does what they can do, everybody asks if they need help — they ask for help, they offer help. All good," she said. "It's just another adventure."

Dangerous conditions are expected throughout the western panhandle, southern Alabama and southern Mississippi, the U.S. National Hurricane Center said. Several counties announced mandatory evacuations while Mobile, Ala., imposed a curfew beginning Friday evening until morning.
Dozens of Waffle Houses closed

In a sign of how serious the warnings are, dozens of Waffle Houses in the Florida Panhandle were closed, according to the company's website. The beloved Southern breakfast chain is known for staying open through severe weather and often is a measuring stick of a storm's severity.
Kelsei Frazier, a Florida-native living in Pace who is no stranger to hurricanes, knows all about the Waffle House Index.

"We joke because if Waffle House is still open, then you know it's not a bad hurricane, but all the Waffle Houses that I know of within at least a normal range from us are closed," said Frazier. "Which is a pretty big deal."
DeSantis warned residents to expect power outages, gasoline shortages and closures of bridges and highways.
The state's National Guard deployed about 5,000 soldiers and airmen to help with the response, and search and rescue teams were ready to respond, while some prisons evacuated inmates.

articles.title: Sara Duterte trial recap, Oct. 9: Unexplained wealth pegged at P818 million
articles.summary: The prosecution presented its final witness against Vice President Sara Duterte on Friday, October 9, a forensic financial analyst who claimed before the Senate impeachment court that the Duterte…

blocks.text: October 10, 2026 | 10:31am

MANILA, Philippines — The prosecution presented its final witness against Vice President Sara Duterte on Friday, October 9, a forensic financial analyst who claimed before the Senate impeachment court that the Duterte couple had a whopping P817.87 million in undeclared assets and income from 2022 to 2025.

Alexander Cabrera, a lawyer and accountant who serves as chairman emeritus of PwC’s Philippine member firm Isla Lipana & Co., said the figure was drawn only from bank, tax, anti-money laundering and corporate records obtained through court subpoenas, and excludes documents held by Duterte and her husband, lawyer Manases Carpio.

The figure is the prosecution’s central claim for Article II, which accuses Duterte of amassing wealth beyond her lawful income, misdeclaring her assets and keeping business interests the Constitution bars her from holding. It is more than eight times the P98.66 million net worth the vice president declared in 2025.
The prosecution has announced it would no longer pursue Article III on bribery, making Cabrera the last witness in its presentation of evidence.

The defense, which will cross-examine Cabrera on Monday, questioned his credibility in making a "supposed" forensic report of the vice president's wealth, based on documents it says should not have been handed over to him.
During its turn in presenting witnesses, the defense will also get their chance to call to the stand their own expert witness.

Earlier in the day, a Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) official confirmed the agency is auditing Duterte and Carpio under letters of authority covering up to 20 years of taxes, and that Cale 88 Foods Corp., a banana chip exporter with ties to Carpio, is also under audit.
Here are three highlights from the proceedings.
1. How the P817.87 million adds up

The prosecution had billed Cabrera as the witness who would make sense of nearly a month of testimony from several bank executives, land registrars, and representatives from the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Anti-Money Laundering Council.
Among them, they put on record huge sums of funds that prosecutors said were missing from Duterte’s SALNs, but none was in a position to say whether it amounted to wealth beyond her lawful income.

Cabrera built his estimated total from four sources: bank balances missing from Duterte’s SALN, undeclared property, bank deposits that exceeded the couple’s declared income, and their share of undeclared income from companies they own.
Duterte and Carpio's undeclared bank balances alone ranged from P23.17 million to P80.70 million a year, most of it in Carpio’s accounts, Cabrera claimed.

Their alleged undeclared property included 17 insurance policies, firearms, real estate and business stakes, he said. Deposits that counted as income totaled P174.96 million from 2022 to 2025, against P63.11 million declared in the couple’s tax returns, he added.

Cabrera also flagged unusual banking activity by the vice president and her husband, the most damning being the manager’s checks worth P96 million allegedly circulated through the couple’s joint account for years before P80 million went into four life insurance policies.

Certain credit card purchases were also flagged as unusual by the witness, such as an alleged single P205,000 payment at the Ginza Inakaya in Tokyo, Japan, as well as two purchases on the same day at Nike SM Davao, totaling more than P300,000.
Cabrera said he counted each asset only once and left out most dollar accounts.
2. Gencorp: over P1 billion in unreported inflows

Cabrera also alleged that Gencorp Industries, a firm Duterte lists in her SALN as a stockholder but whose corporate filings do not name her, left more than P1 billion in bank inflows off its books from 2023 to 2025, equal to 80% to 94% of the revenue it reported.
“Pag ganyan po kalaki ang tinatago niyo, eh fraudulent po iyan (If what you're hiding is that huge, then that is fraudulent),” he said.

Cabrera had cited receipts showing Gencorp runs five Jollibee branches in Davao City despite a capital of only P1.25 million. He attributed 20% of its undeclared income to Duterte, mirroring her stake in Metro City Chow Foods Corp., which shares directors with Gencorp, and called the estimate conservative.
It's Cabrera's theory that Gencorp intentionally kept Duterte’s name off its records because it does business with the Davao City government.
“Kung si VP Sara po ay nakapangalan po sa GIS ng Gencorp, hindi po pwedeng makakuha ng kontrata ang Gencorp po sa City of Davao,” he said.

Her brother, Davao City Mayor Sebastian Duterte, acknowledged in earlier testimony that the city awarded Gencorp 19 contracts worth about P33.2 million and said he would not have allowed them had he known of her stake.

Several senator-judges themselves had done their own math and raised doubts on the truthfulness of Gencorp's filings in their questions to Anne Garcia Marquez, the chief of staff of the BIR's Office of the Commissioner.

Lacson noted Gencorp reported P520.67 million in 2025 sales but paid only P777,093 in income tax. Sen. Kiko Pangilinan said bank records show Gencorp held P46.19 million at the end of 2023, while its audited statements showed only P924,695.
“They were not being truthful if the bank records show that the ending balance in 2023 is 46 million,” Pangilinan says.
The defense, for its part, drew from Marquez that corporations have separate legal personalities and that their income is not the couple’s.
3. Cale88 and money from China
Cabrera claimed Cale88 understated its revenue by an average of 51% a year, and that P193.95 million of its foreign remittances, more than 80%, came from Chinese companies.

Sen. Risa Hontiveros also revealed that based on her team's research, one Ukrainian remitter to Cale88 matches a company under criminal investigation in Kyiv for fraud and money laundering, and that its last transfer to Cale88 came after that case was opened in May 2025.

Sen. Joel Villanueva noted that Cale88 reported P150 million in sales in 2024 with only two employees on record. Marquez said that seemed "impossible" and guessed it would take several machines to power their operations with such a lean workforce.
The BIR’s audit will check whether Cale88 under-declared sales, which could lead to deficiency taxes or, if evasion is proven, a criminal case, she said.
The AMLC’s executive director testified earlier this week that Cale88 could be a money laundering candidate, subject to further investigation.
Overall, Cabrera laid down five main conclusions from his findings:

items: Duterte’s SALNs from 2022 to 2025 “were untruthful";
She “continued to participate in various businesses” as vice president;
Her unexplained wealth amounts to P817.87 million “based only on the limited documents examined";
The violations “establish the pattern of constitutional violations year-on-year";
Other laws, including the Tax Code, “were violated or may have been violated.”

blocks.text: Presiding officer Sen. Chiz Escudero reminded prosecutors that because no subpoena was issued to Cabrera, they must bring him back for cross-examination on Monday, warning that his testimony “would be useless” otherwise.

articles.title: How the trial of two murdered Australian surfers ended in a guilty verdict
articles.summary: The mother of two Australian surfers murdered in Mexico two years ago with their American friend said "accountability matters".

blocks.text: The mother of two murdered Australian surfers, who were killed in Mexico two years ago alongside their American friend, told a court "accountability matters".
Three men have been found guilty of murdering brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, and their US friend Carter Rhoad during a surfing trip in Mexico in 2024.
BBC's Will Grant takes a look at the case.
Read the full story here.

articles.title: Mexico: Court finds three men guilty of murder of Australian, US surfers
articles.summary: The 2024 murders of brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, along with their friend Carter Rhoad, shocked Mexico and drew international outrage.

image.caption: Prosecutors have asked for 210 years of imprisonment for each of the convictsImage: AAP/IMAGO

blocks.text: A Mexican court on Friday convicted three men in the 2024 murders of two Australian brothers and their American friend, who were killed during a botched robbery which sparked international outrage.
Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33, and their friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were on a surfing trip to Mexico when they were shot dead in Baja California state.

They were camping in a remote beachside area near the city of Ensenada when they were attacked during a suspected robbery. Their bodies were found days later, in a well, with gunshot wounds to their heads.
What was said in court?
The judge on Friday ruled that the three Mexican defendants had acted with premeditation. They are yet to be sentenced for the murders.
The prosecution has asked for an "exemplary sentence" of 210 years for each of the three convicted, even though the maximum sentence in Baja California is 60 years.

blocks.caption: The brothers' parents were in court to hear the guilty verdictImage: Guillermo Arias/AFP

blocks.text: Debra Robinson, mother to the Australian brothers, burst into tears when the court passed the guilty verdict.

"While no verdict can ever bring back our boys or ease the heartbreak of losing them," the convictions marked "an important step towards justice and accountability," their father Martin Robinson said in a statement on behalf of the family.
Victim begged for mercy
Case prosecutors described the killings of the three surfers during the closing arguments on Thursday, by recalling the testimony of the girlfriend of one of the main suspects.
She had said that Rhoad had begged for his life while her boyfriend had bragged about "how beautifully" his victims cried before he robbed them.
The triple homicide shocked Mexico and drew international attention when it came to light.
Baja California is one of Mexico's most violent states, riddled with organized crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity doesn't usually affect tourists.

articles.title: US country music star Ella Langley cancels show due to 'security threat'
articles.summary: Police say they checked the concert venue in Tulsa, Oklahoma but "could not find any threat".

blocks.text: US country music star Ella Langley has said she had to cancel her sold-out concert in Tulsa, Oklahoma on Friday night, due to a "serious security threat".
The singer made what she called the "incredibly difficult" decision around two hours before the show at the 19,000-seater arena was due to start.
In a post on Instagram, the 27-year-old said the threat involved "the safety of my fans, the venue staff and my team".
Cpt Richard Meulenberg from Tulsa Police Department said a person had called saying "great harm" would be done at the event with "shots fired and bombs."
He stated his team had checked the venue at BOK Center several times before the show and "could not find any threat".
"The event was ready to go," he added, saying officers with sniffer dogs did a sweep of the arena again after the phone call was made.
"We could not find a credible threat," he said, stressing that the person who had made the call "disrupted this entire event" for thousands of Langley fans.
The star - who did not give any further details - also apologised to her fans, saying additional information regarding ticket refunds "will be shared as soon as possible".

BOK Center issued its own statement, saying that "the safety and well-being of everyone involved is our absolute priority, and after careful consideration, we have determined that the show cannot proceed.
"We understand the disappointment this news brings and apologise to fans who planned to attend."
In September, Langley's country smash Choosin' Texas overtook Mariah Carey's All I Want for Christmas Is You to become the longest-running number one single in US chart history.
Its success helped the singer from Alabama to sweep the Academy of Country Music Awards in May.

articles.title: Trump weighs livestream execution amid bipartisan backlash
articles.summary: Donald Trump said he hasn't decided whether the execution of the Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamed, after the Pentagon announced it would do so. The plan has been criticized by both Republicans…

image.caption: Hasan carried out the deadliest mass shooting on a military base in US history [Undated file photo]Image: Bell County Sheriff's Office/REUTERS

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump said on Friday that Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan "absolutely" deserves the death penalty by firing squad but told reporters he has yet "to make a determination" on whether it will be livestreamed.
"I don't really care how he goes, as long as he goes," Trump said, referring to Hasan.
What did Hegseth and the Pentagon say about Hasan's execution?

Trump's remarks comes a day after the Pentagon said it would livestream the execution of 56-year-old Hasan, a former US Army psychiatrist who murdered 13 people and injured 32 others in Fort Hood in Texas in 2009.

In a video shared by the Pentagon regarding the execution, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public, because people need to understand that there's serious consequence for these types of things."
Hasan is currently being held on death row in Fort Leavenworth in Kansas. His execution is slated for December 3.
He is paralyzed from the waist down and uses a wheelchair after he was shot by an officer responding to the Fort Hood shooting.
JD Vance says he would not watch livestream of execution
US Vice President JD Vance, speaking to reporters in Cincinnati on Friday, also said he doesn't know whether the livestream is "actually going to happen."
"If it is shown publicly," Vance added, "I'm not going to be watching it." Vance is a devout member of the Catholic Church, which opposes the death penalty.
"Whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people," the US vice president said.

blocks.caption: Hasan is incarcerated at the United States Disciplinary Barracks [FILE: September 16, 2026]Image: Paul Hennessy/SOPA Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: Livestream plan faces bipartisan backlash
The Pentagon's plan to broadcast the execution has been met with a fierce backlash from within Trump's own Republican Party and the opposition Democrats.
"I absolutely support the sentence of death, but livestreaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that," said Republican Representative Austin Scott of Georgia.

Public executions are common in Taliban-controlled Afghanistan and the so-called Islamic State (IS) also engaged in public beheadings when the group controlled large swathes of Syria and Iraq in the 2010s. Iran is another country that carries out public executions.
Republican Congressman Rob Bresnahan of Pennsylvania said "an execution shouldn't be a livestreamed spectacle."
"The focus should be on justice for the victims and their families, not turning an execution into entertainment," he said in a statement posted on X. "Their pain deserves respect, not a public show."

Democratic Congressman Eugene Vindman of Virginia, who said he oversaw legal proceedings following the Fort Hood attack, said livestreaming Hasan's execution "is what terrorists and authoritarian regimes do. It's un-American."
Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut said Pentagon chief Hegseth is "turning the Fort Hood execution into a gruesome inhumane spectacle."

The UN human rights office (OHCHR) also strongly condemned the ideaof a livestreamed execution, while the president of the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops called the plana "barbaric promotion of a culture of death."

articles.title: Life-threatening Hurricane Isaias makes landfall in Florida
articles.summary: The storm took direct aim at Florida and is expected to impact Alabama, Georgia, and Louisiana.

blocks.text: Hurricane Isaias has made landfall in the US state of Florida and is expected to bring life-threatening flooding and winds that have forced thousands to evacuate.
The storm weakened slightly to a category 2 hurricane, with 110 mph (175 kph) winds, before ramming into Florida's western panhandle on Friday evening.
Florida, Alabama, and Georgia have each issued states of emergency as meteorologists warned of life-threatening storm surge that could cause up to 9 feet (2.7m) of flooding in some areas.
Isaias is one of three storm systems affecting North America this weekend, with the two others hitting Mexico and Southern California in the El-Niño fuelled warm waters of the Pacific Ocean.
Both Florida and Alabama instituted mandatory evacuations due to the storm.

In Florida, those evacuations includes coastal communities in direct aim of the powerful storm. Florida Senator Rick Scott encouraged residents in designated areas to evacuate as soon as possible, as he warned in a social media post: "DO NOT WAIT! Get out NOW!"
Governor of Alabama Kay Ivey issued a mandatory evacuation for all non-residents, tourists and visitors in key counties likely to be heavily affected by the storm.
Hurricane Isaias is the first hurricane in the Atlantic's hurricane season, which largely has been delayed due to El Niño conditions in the Pacific.
It marks the first time in more than 30 years that a hurricane did not form till October.
The storm is likely to bring "life-threatening storm surge" to the US Gulf Coast, the National Hurricane Center warned.
After hitting Florida, the centre of Isaias is forecast to move across Alabama and into the Tennessee Valley on Saturday and Sunday, the National Weather Service said late on Friday.
As of Friday evening, hurricane-force winds extended outward up to 35 miles (55 km) from Isaias' centre, and tropical storm-force winds extended as far as 205 miles (335 km).
John Guoth, a resident of Navarre, Florida, told the BBC that he and his wife will remain in their home despite the rest of his street having already left.
"It's a hurricane, we get them all the time... we kind of knew that when we moved here," he said.
"Pretty much everything that can fly and will fly is battened down, and everything that cannot fly is really, really secured," he said,
Guoth said he put his ducks and chickens in the bathroom and weighed down his boats and trailers so "nothing flips over".
A few households have remained in the area, describing them as "long-term locals" who are "going to protect our homes".
Pensacola resident Brandin Ruth told the BBC that they have been turning the gas off to the buildings, icing down product and trying to get team members home.
People in the Florida city have "seen bad storms before" but are "bunkering up", he said, adding: "You don't want to underestimate a storm like this".
Two other storms are also forecast to batter North America this weekend.

Hurricane Simon is bearing down on the Pacific coast of Mexico as a category one hurricane. It is set to pick up speed and become category four by Saturday, eventually making landfall near Puerto Vallarta on Sunday, according to Reuters.
Further north, Tropical Storm Rachel, a downgraded hurricane, is heading toward landfall around the US-Mexico border, along the Pacific.
While, Rachel is expected to reach the coast late on Saturday, the impact of the storm is already being felt due to high tides in southern California.
Video footage and photos show several streets under water in Newport Beach, California, through a combination of the tropical storm swells at sea and high tide.
Posting on its account on X, the City of Newport Beach advised people to "avoid the Balboa Peninsula due to street flooding caused by recent storm conditions and elevated tides".
It also urged people not to drive through flooded streets. Bulldozers have been shoring up the beach to try and prevent further flooding.
With additional reporting by Simon King.

articles.title: Trump fumes over Nobel peace prize snub and criticizes Norway
articles.summary:
President complains about not winning prize in year he started war with Iran and says: ‘We will not forget, Norway’

Donald Trump complained Friday about not winning the Nobel peace prize for…

blocks.text: Donald Trump complained Friday about not winning the Nobel peace prize for 2026, a year in which he started a war with Iran.
At what was supposed to be a rally for other Republican candidates in Syracuse, New York, the US president devoted a long portion of his speech airing his grievances with the Nobel committee.

“The United States of America, represented by me as your president, should have received the Nobel peace prize, but didn’t. And this is an indelible stain on the country of Norway, and those people that made such a disgraceful and embarrassing decision,” Trump said.

“The Nobel peace prize has been forever discredited by a handful of radical ideologues who are anti-democracy and really enemies of civilization,” Trump went on. “We will not forget, Norway, that you didn’t give this prize.”

Trump also recited a list of wars he claims to have settled, some of which were not wars and some that are still not settled, before adding: “I’m about to settle or win two more: Iran and Russia-Ukraine.”
Trump said he would be ending both wars “quickly”.
“I will tell you what,” he added, darkly. “Iran will be very quick one way or the other: that they give us everything or they don’t exist any longer.”

“Additionally, I stopped Iran from having a nuclear weapon and blowing up the entire Middle East and ultimately far beyond the Middle East, including Europe, perhaps the US and I saved more lives than anyone in history,” Trump claimed, despite the fact that US intelligence agencies reported to Congress in 2025 that Iran had actually suspended its pursuit of nuclear weapons in 2003.

“Despite all of this and all of these unbelievable accomplishments, the Nobel prize was given out today to a liberal person who works at the United Nations, who nobody has ever heard of,” Trump said of Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.

articles.title: Hurricane Isaias makes landfall in Florida with severe effects expected across several states
articles.summary:
Governors of Mississippi, Alabama and Florida declared states of emergency as a downsized Fema faces first major test

Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, on Friday evening,…

blocks.text: Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, on Friday evening, sweeping ashore from the northern Gulf of Mexico as the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season.
The National Hurricane Center (NHC) in Miami said the center of the cyclone made landfall at 9.30pm ET as a category 2 hurricane.
Forecasters had expected Isaias to weaken from its peak earlier on Friday as a major category 3 hurricane due to shifts in wind speed.
But even as high-end category 2 storm, the NHC said, severe impacts would be felt across a wide stretch of the northern Gulf coast from Louisiana to Florida, and far inland.
They included a “life-threatening” storm surge of up to 7ft (2.1 meters) along the Alabama-Florida line, and powerful wind gusts reaching parts of northern Georgia.

“Weakening will occur after landfall, but sustained hurricane-force winds will likely occur near and along Isaias’s track up to 100 miles inland,” wrote Robbie Berg, an NHC hurricane expert, in a Friday advisory.

The governors of Mississippi, Alabama, and Florida all declared states of emergency ahead of the storm’s arrival, urging some residents of coastal communities to evacuate and many more to prepare for the storm’s likely violent arrival.
The Mobile office of the National Weather Service warned parts of Florida could see “extremely dangerous” tornado-like winds.
By Friday evening, more than 400,000 customers had lost power across Alabama and Florida, according to poweroutage.com.
“Things are going to get really, really treacherous,” Jamie Rhome, deputy director for the National Hurricane Center, told the AP.

Florida’s national guard deployed roughly 5,000 soldiers and airmen to aid with the response, the AP reported. Some prisons were also evacuating their incarcerated populations. Most flights were grounded at several airports in Florida’s Panhandle.

Isaias is notable as one of the two latest-forming Atlantic hurricanes on record, tying a record set on 8 October 1905. None of the eight previous named storms of the 2026 Atlantic season intensified above tropical storm status.
Ahead of the storm, oil and gas producers shut down a significant share of offshore production in the Gulf, which accounts for almost 15% of crude pumped annually in the US.

The storm could also be the first major test of the ability of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) to deploy a large workforce after huge cuts and restructuring, emergency management experts warned.

The Trump administration has said it wants to eliminate, or drastically downsize, Fema. More than 4,300 employees left the agency in fiscal year 2025, about 17% of the workforce, according to a recent US government accountability office (GAO) report.

articles.title: Powerful 7.7 magnitude earthquake rocks Panama
articles.summary: A magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck southern Panama on Friday, damaging buildings and sending thousands into the streets, but the country appeared to escape widespread destruction or deaths.

blocks.text: World·New
A magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck southern Panama on Friday, damaging buildings and sending thousands into the streets, but the country appeared to escape widespread destruction or deaths.
Country appears to have escaped widespread destruction or deaths
Powerful earthquake hits Panama, triggers tsunami warnings

The ‌U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) said the earthquake hit at a depth of 12.6 kilometres, with an epicentre in a sparsely populated area about 200 kilometres from the capital, and that some casualties were possible.

In the following hours, even as more than 40 aftershocks rattled the isthmus nation, the Panama Canal and Cobre Panama copper mine reported normal operations and the Tocumen International Airport lifted ​a suspension on flights.
Office workers in the upscale business hub of downtown Panama City ​fretted about how to get home in the snarl of traffic, after the quake sent thousands into the streets.
Juan Sanchez, a 37-year-old Economy Ministry employee, waited for a bus he said he doubted would arrive.
Canadian in Panama experiences aftershock live on air | Hanomansing Live
"They evacuated all of ​these buildings. Everyone is outside. Now the problem is, how do we get home?"
President Raul Mulino travelled to Penonome, ⁠a city about halfway between the epicentre ⁠and Panama City, where some buildings collapsed and a church was damaged.

items: Some TV meteorologists want to talk about climate change. Not everyone wants to hear it

blocks.text: Despite the ‌force of Friday's tremor, the country appeared to have been spared the destruction of other recent powerful quakes in the region, with no deaths or injuries immediately reported.
Back-to-back quakes in Venezuela in June killed several thousand people, while a quake in Colombia in August killed more than 300.
Cars are seen crushed under a collapsed building after an earthquake in Penonome, Panama, on Friday. (Martin Bernetti/AFP/Getty Images)

An exposure report by the USGS estimated about 43,000 Panamanians lived in areas with at least severe exposure ⁠to the quake. This compares with nearly 1.4 million in the area of the twin quakes in Venezuela and over 1.6 million in the quake-hit zone of western Colombia.
Nestor Luque, director of Panama's geosciences institute, attributed the quake to the Azuero Sona Fault System that he said contained a massive buildup of pressure ‌that is occasionally released.
"The seismic signals have travelled throughout the national territory and that is why it could be felt everywhere."
People gather on a street in Panama City after an earthquake on Friday. (Enea Lebrun/Reuters)
In Panama City, Luque said he counted 40 seconds of vibrations, though other areas may have felt even longer tremors.
Sabina Rios, who was on the sixth floor of an old U.S. military-era building in Panama City, said the shaking was unusually strong and prolonged.
"The quake felt strong ​and lasted a long time, the longest I've felt in years," Rios said.
People look at a damaged government building in Penonome on Friday. (Martin Bernetti/AFP/Getty Images)

Victor Pinzon, a 48-year-old maintenance worker, told Reuters he had watched high-rise window cleaners ride out the shaking. "It's a miracle they didn't ⁠get killed," he said. "They looked like they were swinging in a hammock."
Strong earthquakes are not common in Panama, and some elderly residents were in ⁠tears as they evacuated into the streets.

"We're scared. It's just the two of us old folks here. The house has cracked, and we're afraid ⁠it ⁠could fall on us," said Ricardo Brown, 74, in Herrera ​province in southern Panama, where he said he saw a number of damaged homes.
A statue is seen by the earthquake in Penonome on Friday. (Martin Bernetti/AFP/Getty Images)

Omar Smith, who heads Panama's civil protection agency, told news outlet Telemetro Reporta ​that impacts had also been reported in Chitre, ⁠the capital of Herrera, and along the coast in Los Santos province.
The USGS estimated economic losses could amount to 1 to 10 per cent of Panama's gross domestic product, and electricity provider Naturgy reported power outages in six provinces.
Panama was due to hold a national evacuation drill on Monday of next week to test the country's emergency response.

Nearly 70 potential contacts have been placed under quarantine in Nairobi
A Kenyan businessman was able to spend time in one of the regions worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified.

The 40-year-old - who was only diagnosed with the deadly infectious disease after arriving seriously ill at a Nairobi hospital - became Kenya's first confirmed case. He died two days later on 5 October.

That his infection went undetected at multiple health facilities in the Democratic Republic of Congo and two airport health screenings in Uganda and Kenya has raised serious questions about these nations' biosecurity during a significant outbreak.
More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date.

Africa CDC, the continent's leading public health agency, has now reconstructed the Kenyan patient's movements across nearly six weeks, revealing several missed opportunities to detect his infection and potentially preventing dozens of people from coming into contact with the deadly virus.
DR Congo

The account, presented by the agency's emergency director, Dr Wessam Mankoula, provides the clearest picture yet of how the businessman travelled thousands of kilometres while growing increasingly unwell.
The man, whose identity has not been made public, had lived in DR Congo for seven years and had travelled across three of its provinces on business.
Exactly when or where he contracted Ebola remains unclear - but it was present in all three provinces he went through by early October, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
The man had spent much of late August and early September in the province of Bas-Uélé, visiting towns including Buta, Aketi and Likati.

blocks.caption: A map showing the man's journey from DR Congo through Uganda to Kenya

blocks.text: The WHO confirmed an Ebola case in Buta in August, prior to his visit, though there is no evidence he contracted the virus there.
His symptoms first emerged around 15 September. He was given antibiotics and sent home.
Two days later, he was admitted to the Tongo Etandi Health Centre in Bondo, where he remained until 19 September.
Despite suffering from fever and a rash, he was diagnosed with a skin infection.

Without an Ebola test being taken at any point during his travels, it is hard to say exactly when he contracted the virus. Those symptoms are consistent with the early stages of the disease, but also other infections common to the region, such as malaria.
On 20 September, he flew to Kisangani, a city with a population of about 1.5 million people on the Congo River, where he spent more than 10 days seeking medical care.
We do not know which hospitals or clinics treated him there, nor what medications they gave him. Kisangani is the capital of Tshopo province which has only recorded 51 Ebola cases.
Uganda
However, on 1 October, more than two weeks after first becoming ill, the businessman boarded another domestic flight to Beni, before continuing his journey to Kasindi, a busy border town.
Both Beni and Kasindi are in North Kivu, which has recorded 1,755 Ebola infections and more than 1,000 deaths, making it one of the Congolese provinces worst-hit by the disease.
But he did not stay there long, crossing into Uganda later that day.
Uganda imposed restrictions on movement across its border with DR Congo shortly after the outbreak began in May.

The country has experience containing several Ebola outbreaks, including through surveillance, contact tracing and the isolation of suspected cases. It has had some cases this year - mostly among people travelling from DR Congo - but was declared free of the disease in August.
But the border between the two nations stretches for hundreds of kilometres through remote terrain, making it difficult to police.
It remains unclear whether the businessman passed through an official health checkpoint when he crossed the border.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The man's funeral was held under strict safety protocols

blocks.text: The man's funeral was held under strict safety protocols
Once he had, he travelled by road to the capital, Kampala, and then Entebbe International Airport, where he boarded a flight to Nairobi on 3 October.

Ugandan officials said his temperature was normal when he passed through airport screening. Health experts say his case highlights the limitations of relying on temperature checks and self-declarations.
Mankoula said investigators were examining whether the man's medication could have suppressed his temperature. He may have also not had a fever when he passed through the checks.
Kenya

Similarly, he was not flagged as a suspected Ebola patient when he reached Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, where a relative collected him and drove him directly to Nairobi Hospital, a private medical facility in the Kenyan capital.
By then, he was suffering from fever, chills, muscle pain, a sore throat and bleeding.
Laboratory tests confirmed that he had contracted the Bundibugyo species of Ebola - the same one responsible for the outbreak in DR Congo.
He was placed in isolation while his condition deteriorated. He died on 5 October and was buried the following day under strict infection-control measures.

The Kenyan government says it has now identified 66 people who may have been in contact with him after he arrived there. The WHO says the number is likely to rise as contact-tracing in Uganda and DR Congo continues.
The quarantine arrangements have also raised concerns among some healthcare workers, amid questions about how the patient was handled at Nairobi Hospital.
Kenya's health ministry says more than 652,000 travellers have been screened and nearly 5,000 healthcare workers trained to deal with Ebola, with five facilities designated to handle cases.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person who has developed symptoms, or through contaminated materials.
Its incubation period ranges from two to 21 days, meaning someone exposed to the virus may not become ill until several weeks later.
CDC advice
Mankoula urged travellers experiencing symptoms of Ebola to report them, saying early medical attention could improve their chances of survival.
"When you reveal any Ebola-related symptoms early, you're not only preventing the virus spreading to other countries but you're also protecting yourself first," he said.
The WHO has warned that stigma surrounding Ebola could discourage people from reporting symptoms or seeking medical care, potentially allowing the virus to spread undetected.

The agency says it is stepping up efforts to encourage this by reducing fear and misinformation about the disease - something that is a big problem in DR Congo, where some health workers have been attacked by people who claim Ebola doesn't exist.

articles.title: Zelenskyy furious as Trump announces deal to buy Russian diesel
articles.summary: President says deal essential to lower US fuel prices but move set to create fresh crisis with Ukraine and Nato allies

blocks.text: Donald Trump was on a fresh collision course with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and European allies on Friday after a stunning agreement to buy Russian diesel, upending years of US and western pressure on the Kremlin to end its four-and-a-half year war against Ukraine.
Zelenskyy reacted furiously to Trump’s announcement of the deal with President Vladimir Putin of Russia, calling it “absolutely terrible” and “not fair and not honest”.

In a move likely to create a fresh crisis with Washington’s Nato allies, Trump announced the deal with Putin on his Truth Social network, saying it was essential to reduce fuel prices in the US, which have soared as a result of his decision to go to war with Iran.

“I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter,” Trump wrote.
“Based on the condition of their diesel refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 tons of diesel fuel.”

He added: “Diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my greatest priority.”

Fuel prices have rocketed due to Iran’s closure of the strait of Hormuz, a strategically sensitive choke point that was the passageway for 20% of the global oil supplies before the war. While costs have risen for motorists – with a gallon of fuel now averaging $4.20 – it is the soaring price of diesel, which last month rose to a record high of $6.52, that has inflicted the most political damage to Trump and the Republicans as November’s midterm approach.
Diesel is the main supply chain fuel, and a rise in its costs feeds into consumer prices and also hurts US farmers, who need to operate machinery.

The agreement was criticized by Democrats, who said it undercut a law Trump signed last month allowing for a broad range of sanctions on Russian banks, officials and tankers, as well as directing him to impose steep tariffs on the top five importers of oil or natural gas from Russia. The law gave Trump wide discretion to make exception to its provisions.
But the fiercest response came from Zelenskyy, who told Axios that it “looks like a a happy birthday present for Putin. It looks absolutely terrible.” The Russian leader turned 74 earlier this week.

In a long social media post, Zelenskyy, who has had an uneasy relationship with Trump, said the deal amounted to an “an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged”. Russia was likely to repay it with “further terror and perfidy”.
“It plays into Russia’s hands – allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world,” he said.
Trump announced the oil deal as his envoys, Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner, met with Ukrainian and European officials in Miami to discuss proposals to end the war.

Zelenskyy, in a separate statement released by Ukraine’s embassy in Washington on Friday, said the Ukrainian negotiators had been “used as a smokescreen for the deal” which he called “a weak decision by strong partners”.
“That is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other.” he said.

Trump has recently criticized Ukraine for attacking Russian diesel refineries, calling on Zelenskyy to choose alternative targets. The Ukrainian leader rejected the request unless Russia accepted a reciprocal de-escalation plan that would stop Moscow attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.

The agreement also comes on the heels of rising tensions between Russia and Washington’s Nato allies in Europe, amid speculation that Moscow might be preparing military action intended to test the alliance’s resolve.

The latest development is likely to lead to a further deterioration of Zelenskyy’s relationship with the Trump administration. He was infamously ambushed by Trump and the vice president, JD Vance, last year in an explosive White House encounter when the president told him: “You don’t have the cards.”
But Trump has since reportedly grown disenchanted with Putin, expressing disappointment in his failure to reach a deal.

Trump’s willingness to reach an agreement with Putin that will lower fuel costs comes despite Russia’s support for Iran in its war with the US. Russia is believed to have given Iran satellite intelligence and overhead surveillance data detailing the locations of American forces, ships, aircraft and military bases. It has also provided drone component and ammunition.

articles.title: Sandiganbayan allows Romualdez to sign pre-trial order at QC Payatas Jail on Oct. 12
articles.summary: The Sandiganbayan Third Division granted the motion of former Speaker and incumbent Leyte 1st District Representative Martin Romualdez to sign the pre-trial order at the New Quezon City Jail in…

blocks.text: Published October 10, 2026 7:37am Updated October 10, 2026 7:41am

The Sandiganbayan Third Division granted the motion of former Speaker and incumbent Leyte 1st District Representative Martin Romualdez to sign the pre-trial order at the New Quezon City Jail in Payatas on Monday, October 12.
The anti-graft court earlier ordered Romualdez to appear before it on October 12 for the first day of his bail hearing.
A pre-trial order is issued after the pre-trial conference or the court process where the evidence for both parties are marked, read.
The Office of the Ombudsman filed last September 7 a P7.4-billion plunder charge against Romualdez and three others over their alleged involvement in a kickback scheme on flood control projects.
The former speaker was arrested and underwent booking procedures on the same day while confined at the Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City.
He was brought to the New Quezon City Jail in Payatas, Quezon City on September 14 where he has since been detained.
Romualdez, in a videoconference on September 16, pleaded not guilty to the charges.
He filed a petition for bail on September 28, and said the Ombudsman’s evidence against him are only enough to raise suspicions, rather than certainty, and not enough to keep him detained
These insufficient evidence, Romualdez said, include:

items: the accounts of former DPWH Undersecretary Roberto Bernardo and former Bulacan First District Engineer Henry Alcantara ("Alcantara") concerning alleged dealings with his co-accused and former House appropriations panel chaiperson Elizaldy "Zaldy" Co of Ako Bicol party-list over contractor "commitments"
the statements of eight security aides of accused Co, three of whom have since recanted, describing the transport of luggage to properties said to be associated with accused Romualdez
accusing Romualdez of involvement by virtue of his office as Speaker of the House of Representatives and the passage of appropriations measures in the ordinary course of legislation; and
the corporate and financial transactions of a certain Jose Paras and of companies in which Paras is the principal shareholder.

blocks.text: “None of them strongly establishes accused Romualdez’s knowing participation in the alleged scheme or his acquisition of its proceeds. Bernardo and Alcantara describe dealings with accused Co. The security aides describe the movement of luggage and, on a few occasions, the sight of cash, but not its source, its amount, or its receipt by accused Romualdez,” the bail petition read.
In addition, Romualdez said that the prosecution’s evidence does not show his knowledge, direction, or benefit as with his participation in the racketeering scheme.
Romualdez’s petition also asked the Sandiganbayan to fix a reasonable amount of bail, with such sureties as the anti-graft court may require. —with a report from JP Soriano/KG, GMA News

articles.title: 'Everyone hates the police' – what France's school protests reveal about a divided nation
articles.summary: Students taking to the streets in France have become a focal point in the country's increasingly polarised politics.

blocks.text: 'Everyone hates the police' – what France's school protests reveal about a divided nation
Image source, Getty Images
Hundreds of thousands of students have protested across France since the end of last month
ByNick Beake
Europe correspondent
As dustbins burn and students chant "everyone hates the police" in the French city of Lille, one teenager explains why he and his friends have taken to the streets.
"There aren't even enough chairs. We have to go and find some at the start of every lesson," the 16-year-old, who did not want to give his name, says of his school.
"We've got 50 minutes to eat at lunchtime but there are 2,000 of us that need to get through the canteen."

He is one of hundreds of thousands of students who have protested across France since the end of last month over staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées, secondary schools attended by 15 to 18-year-olds.
Despite the government's apparent attempts to make concessions, the students show no sign of backing down.
"They have armies, they have the police, they have the powers," says Massicella, 18, as she marches through Lille. "But we have the mass population."

The protests, which have turned violent, have become a focal point in France's polarised politics, with all sides accusing the other of escalating tensions. As a presidential election approaches, politicians on both the hard right and hard left have sought to capitalise on the unrest and on what many see as the government's inability to resolve the crisis.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Massicella, second left, and her friends have been protesting in Lille

blocks.text: Massicella, second left, and her friends have been protesting in Lille
The protests - ignited at the Lycée Antoine-de-Saint-Exupéry in the deprived Paris suburb of Créteil - have struck a chord across the country.

Videos of rats scuttling through corridors in other lycées soon hit social media, providing striking symbols of the discontent. Other videos on TikTok and Instagram showed broken toilets, holes in walls and mouldy ceilings across the country. Students have complained of unbearable heat in the summer and freezing classrooms in the winter.
The anger has also focused on long school hours, chronic staff shortages, overcrowded classes and a deeply unpopular university admissions system.
Watch: Marseille school students explain why they're protesting

The problem for the French government - which became clearer as we spoke to dozens of pupils this week - is that even if a tiny minority of schools have a problem with rodents, a very large number of pupils believe their own education is failing them.
On Tuesday, the government said 250,000 people marched, most of them young. The trade unions said it was more like half a million.
But it is not just students taking to the streets - their teachers are joining them.
Secondary school teacher Marine Monins, who joined the demonstrations in Lille, shows us a laminated timetable which she says illustrates the problem.
It has become normal for pupils to start at 8am and finish as late as 6pm, but the days are punctuated by hours-long gaps because of bad planning and staff shortages.
When lessons do go ahead, the classes are typically packed with 35 pupils (by comparison, the average secondary school class in England has fewer than 23 pupils).
"It's now impossible to give every child the attention they deserve," Monins explains.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Teachers, including Marine Monins and Marjorie Roussel, have joined their students in calling for change

blocks.text: Teachers, including Marine Monins and Marjorie Roussel, have joined their students in calling for change
On Thursday, the French government made its first sign of ceding ground to protesters, with a promise of 3,000 extra supply teachers in the coming days.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has said by the end of October there will be a plan unveiled to respond to the crisis. Ministers have said they could look again at resources for schools within next year's squeezed budget.
But this has been met with a collective shrug at barricaded school gates across the country.
"It goes beyond having decent toilets in schools," lycée student Alcidor says in Paris, under the statue of Marianne at Place de la République, a place synonymous with protest.
"It's strong anger from the youth in France that doesn't feel represented, that feels abandoned, that feels unheard and is scared of what's coming in the future."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Police have been accused of heavy-handed tactics

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Police have been accused of heavy-handed tactics
The unrest has resulted in widespread arrests and injuries.
So far, almost 7,000 people have been detained during the disorder with more than 85% being children, according to the interior ministry.
More than 700 police officers have been injured in the past three weeks.

But rights groups and unions accuse the police of resorting to heavy-handed tactics against minors, including the use of batons, tear gas and non-lethal flash-ball guns. At least 200 pupils have been injured, along with dozens of teachers.
A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation between police and demonstrators in the northern city of Lens.

Reports of how the teenager sustained the injury differ. A police union source cited by the AFP news agency said the boy appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police, which then exploded in his hand. However, a witness told local media that the teenager did not pick up the grenade.
A teacher at the boy's school, Bastien Riez, who is also a union rep, believes that current police tactics could irrevocably damage the relationship with France's youth.

"For many, this is their first experience of democracy and protest, and they are met with police and a sham of social dialogue and democracy. I fear that many young people will stop believing in this so-called democracy altogether."
Police have since been banned from using stun grenades at school protests.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Kaspar says strangers have been hijacking some protests

blocks.text: Kaspar says strangers have been hijacking some protests

But Parisian pupil Kaspar, 15, speaks of his fear when coming face-to-face with police in full riot gear. He says he and his friends have been protesting peacefully, but strangers were hijacking their protests.
"These people are coming just to shoot fireworks at police officers and they run. This is not the message we want to send to the world."
Police chiefs say violence, directed by agitators who have no link to the schools, is making their job incredibly hard.

Michel Chaballier, deputy secretary-general of the National Police Commissioners' Union (SCPN), says he fears the "political climate has been radicalised", and it was more and more difficult to have a calm, constructive public debate ahead of the national vote next spring.

"Police officers find themselves caught in the middle of this social tension, which is sometimes fuelled by irresponsible politicians," he says. "That's a shame, because I think this country deserves better."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Marine Le Pen has condemned damage to schools

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Marine Le Pen has condemned damage to schools
The protests have become another bruising battleground in France's culture wars, with leaders of the hard left and right seeking to capitalise.
More than three-quarters of under-30s in France interviewed for an Ipsos survey conducted for Aix-Marseille University this week said they were worried about the state of their country.
But many people have a more profound and wider concern about just how dramatically the middle ground in France is eroding, leaving a chasm in the political landscape.
The education crisis is symptomatic of this but also threatens to act as an accelerant.
Most polling suggests more and more French citizens are looking to political extremes for answers to their problems – whether they are linked to education, the economy, identity or immigration.
Marine Le Pen of the hard right National Rally is the frontrunner in the 2027 presidential race.
Next, neck and neck, are Édouard Philippe and Jean-Luc Mélenchon.
Philippe was a prime minister in President Emmanuel Macron's first term and has since founded a centre-right party called Horizons.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Jean-Luc Mélenchon has been supportive of the demonstrations

blocks.text: Jean-Luc Mélenchon has been supportive of the demonstrations
Jean-Luc Mélenchon, a veteran hard-left politician and founder of France Unbowed (LFI), has been a prominent older face among the students at rallies over the past three weeks.
Opponents have accused him of provoking and profiting from the unrest, while he counters that only his party truly represents the French youth.

He claims the current movement that has emerged from the schools protest is the most potent since 1968, when huge demonstrations almost brought down the government of President Charles de Gaulle. At its height, 10 million workers were on the streets before fresh elections led to the revolt fizzling out, but not before carving an indelible memory in French social history.
Despite being born more than four decades later, an exasperated generation of French teenagers are looking to the past for inspiration.
"I personally want to reproduce 1968!" Massicella declares in Lille, as she nears the end of the protest march.
Le Pen has stayed away from the protests and her most notable interventions have come in condemning the damage to schools, which is said to run into the millions of euros.
She has also suggested that parents of children who have committed the vandalism should pay for repairs.
The principle of casseur-payeur – those who break have to pay – has been an impassioned topic that has dominated French media this week.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The 1968 protests have carved an indelible memory in French social history

blocks.text: The 1968 protests have carved an indelible memory in French social history
The problem for President Macron is that there is no quick fix.

This is not a scenario where there is an unpopular piece of legislation that can be withdrawn in a hasty reverse ferret the prime minister is tasked with performing. That was the case with the gilets jaunes – the relentless protest in high vis jackets over a fuel tax rise nearly a decade ago.
Wholesale reform of the education system would cost billions – in new classrooms, new facilities, new teachers – and take years to achieve.
And changes that may seem more easily done – such as a reduction of the length of the school day – would be hugely problematic to implement logistically.
What is more, any proposals which appease the students and end the current protests would have to be agreed at a time when France's finances are in a mess.

The cost of servicing the national debt each year has now exceeded the core state education budget. Under the 2027 draft budget, there will be a 1.7% rise in education spending - but this is an under-inflation increase.
Le Pen has vowed to cut public spending even further if she enters the Élysée Palace.
She is banking that her promises to cut debt, curb migration and restrict certain benefits to French citizens will eclipse any criticism over her position on the protesting pupils.
For her, discipline, a traditional curriculum and pride in France's history should be the defining features of every classroom.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Many students have said they will not back down from protesting

blocks.text: Many students have said they will not back down from protesting
But many students are showing little sign of backing down from another French tradition.
"In France, we have this tradition and history of revolting," says Alcidor in Paris.
"That's the way we gained our rights and the way we will always gain them. That's our spirit."
As the rain came outside the Lycée Voltaire central in Paris this week, the reality of having been up early once again to block the main gate started to kick in and the energy of the crowd dipped.
But not for long.
A huge cheer erupted as a senior teacher unlocked the hulking front door and poked her head out into the street.
"The canteen is still open."
The hunger for better schools among France's youth and better days for everyone else will not be so easily sated.
Additional reporting by Bruno Boelpaep and Manon Prat

articles.title: Trump names new press secretary to succeed Karoline Leavitt
articles.summary: Trump has appointed Katie Zacharia to take over the White House press secretary role vacated by Karoline Leavitt. She assumes the role with Trump struggling with low approval ratings driven by the US…

image.caption: Leavitt (right) was a staunch Trump supporter [FILE: July 15, 2025]Image: Manuel Balce Ceneta/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump on Friday announced that Katie Zacharia will be the next White House press secretary, succeeding Karoline Leavitt.
Zacharia is a 'loyal and brilliant supporter,' Trump says

In a post on his Truth Social network, Trump said it was a "great honor" to appoint Zacharia to the role, calling her a "loyal and brilliant supporter" and member of the Make America Great Again movement.

Zacharia, a 42-year-old native of California, had been serving as Senior Communications Advisor to Truth Social. She had also earlier worked as Deputy Assistant Secretary for Public Affairs at the Department of Homeland Security.
Zacharia, in a post on X, thanked Trump and said "his leadership is a blessing to this country."

"The work ahead is to continue delivering strong results for our country and communicating to the American people the major wins that the administration is making every single day," Zacharia said. "I look forward to working with the White House press corps, and with reporters across the country, to get that record out."
Zacharia said her predecessor Leavitt was "fabulous" and that she set a "high standard" to meet for the press secretary job.
Karoline Leavitt to quit as White House press secretary
Will Zacharia follow Leavitt's combative approach?
Trump had announced that Leavitt would resign in August to spend more time with her young children and family.
Earlier this week, conservative-leaning broadcaster Fox News announced that Leavitt would provide commentary on the network starting from November 1.
Leavitt took a combative approach to questions from the White House press corps during her tenure as press secretary.

In January, she called a White House reporter a "left-wing hack" after a question regarding the fatal US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) shooting of American citizen Renee Good in Minneapolis. She also had to defend Trump's controversial handling of the Epstein files and the ongoing Iran war.

Leavitt managed to stay in the role for over 18 months — a long tenure for a high-stress job under a demanding president. During Trump's first term from 2017 to 2021, he had four press secretaries: Sean Spicer, Sarah Huckabee Sanders, Stephanie Grisham and Kayleigh McEnany.

Zacharia's tenure comes as Trump faces low approval ratings due to high energy prices amid the Iran war and the looming midterms on November 3, where the opposition Democrats are expected to make major congressional gains.
Trump vs. the press: Who controls the story?

articles.title: Women with PMOS should get subsidised weight loss drugs, advocates say
articles.summary:
With GLP-1s to treat the condition not specifically approved by the TGA, patients are being prescribed them off-label

  • Get our

blocks.text: Women living with a chronic hormonal condition should have access to taxpayer-funded weight loss medications, advocates say.
The Polyendrocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome Association of Australia (POSAA) is urging for GLP-1 drugs to be approved on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme for people living with the condition.
Formerly known as polycystic ovarian syndrome, PMOS affects one in eight women. Symptoms can include irregular periods, excess hair growth on the body and face, weight gain, and hair thinning.
The lifelong condition, for which there is no cure, can lead to an increased risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and endometrial cancer.
While GLP-1s are not specifically approved by the Therapeutic Goods Administration to treat PMOS, patients are being prescribed the medications off-label.
Half a million Australians are estimated to be using weight-loss medications regularly, a UNSW study found in July.

Lorna Berry, a spokesperson for the POSAA who was diagnosed with the condition at 32, said she would welcome GLP-1s being subsidised for patients diagnosed with PMOS, in addition to funding for evidence-based research.
“It’s important for people to have access to medications, irrespective of where they live or where they were born … it’s really important that there’s equitable access,” she told the Guardian.

Berry said some women living with the condition were already missing out on being able to access the medications due to their high cost, which can set patients back several hundred dollars each month.

Associate professor Magdalena Simonis, the women’s health spokesperson for the Royal Australasian College of Physicians, said the college did not currently have a position on whether GLP-1s were appropriate for the management of PMOS.

“They’re not necessarily the only tool we have available to us, and that is important because long-term use is expensive, and it doesn’t look like these are going to be on the PBS anytime soon, and maybe not ever for conditions such as PMOS,” she said.
“Because traditionally women’s conditions are not included in these changes.”
Simonis, a GP with an expert interest in PMOS, said should research find the weight-loss medications more effective than existing treatments, a broader discussion about health equity would be needed.
“That is a conversation that we’re having about obesity as a national issue,” she said.
GLP-1 drugs – glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists – mimic a naturally occurring hormone which helps manage blood sugar levels and reduces hunger.
after newsletter promotion
Ozempic is listed by the PBS, but only for the treatment of diabetes.
The Pharmaceutical Benefits Advisory Committee last November recommended Wegovy be subsidised for those with a body mass index above 35.
The committee will meet next month when it will consider Novo Nordisk’s revised proposal to list Wegovy for obesity following protracted negotiations.
The Danish pharmaceutical company produces both Ozempic and Wegovy.
They contain the same active ingredient – semaglutide – but Wegovy has a higher dose.
“Novo Nordisk is continuing to work constructively with the Department of Health to try to negotiate a solution for the PBS listing of Wegovy,” a company spokesperson said.
“We remain committed to improving access for eligible Australians living with obesity.”

QENDO, an organisation advocating for people affected by PMOS and other women’s health conditions, said it recognised “growing interest in GLP-1 medications for managing PMOS, particularly for people experiencing metabolic complications and challenges with weight management”.

“While emerging evidence suggests potential benefits for some patients, further research is needed to establish their long-term effectiveness and safety specifically for PMOS,” QENDO’s acting chief executive, Kate Fisher, said.
