articles.title: Ex-Marineland beluga whale dies in Chicago aquarium
articles.summary: Shedd Aquarium in Chicago says Caspian, a 27-year-old female beluga, died on Wednesday, becoming the sixth animal from the closed Ontario theme park Marineland to die after a massive relocation of…

image.caption: Visitors look at beluga whales at the Shedd Aquarium in Chicago in November 2012. The aquarium says Caspian, a 27-year-old female beluga relocated from now-defunct Ontario-based Marineland, died on Wednesday despite efforts to save her. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New

Shedd Aquarium in Chicago says Caspian, a 27-year-old female beluga, died on Wednesday, becoming the sixth animal from the closed Ontario theme park Marineland to die after a massive relocation of whales and dolphins over the summer.
4 other belugas, 1 dolphin have also died after relocation from closed Canadian theme park
Another whale shipped out of Marineland has died at the Shedd Aquarium in Chicago.
The aquarium says Caspian, a 27-year-old female beluga, died on Wednesday despite efforts to save her.
It's the sixth animal from the closed Niagara Falls, Ont., theme park to die after a massive relocation of whales and dolphins over the summer.
Four other belugas and one dolphin from Marineland have died since they were moved out of the former tourist attraction.

items: 4 Marineland belugas, 1 dolphin, died after being transferred. Why the rest remain on 'death watch'
'Emergency rescue' of Marineland's beluga whales to U.S. aquariums has begun

blocks.text: Shedd says Caspian had not been eating properly and blood samples showed abnormalities in her electrolyte levels. The park added that her blood had become "dangerously acidic."
The aquarium says those findings helped the veterinary care team understand how sick the beluga was, but they did not establish a cause of death.
Shedd says Caspian was on life support for nearly four hours before she died.
Why Marineland's last living belugas are on 'death watch'
Shedd recently performed necropsies on Peekachu and Rain, two other Marineland whales that died there, and concluded that they had chronic, pre-existing diseases.
Shedd and four other aquariums in the United States and Spain helped Marineland relocate all 30 of its belugas and four dolphins over the course of six weeks this summer.
Marineland had said it was running out of money and could no longer care for the last captive whales and dolphins in Canada.
A beluga named Jelly Bean and a dolphin named Echo died at Oceanografic Valencia in Spain after the move.

articles.title: Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices
articles.summary: The US president hopes to ease his party's pain before next month's midterm elections, writes the BBC's North America correspondent.

blocks.text: Donald Trump's decision to import Russian fuel to the US represents a remarkable about-face from the president.
Just three weeks ago, Trump signed legislation to authorise fresh American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas.
Now, Trump says, Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel to the US and world markets in the coming months.
The deal comes as Trump is still grappling with the political fallout of the Iran war and its impact on global energy prices, weeks before American voters head to the polls in the midterm elections.
As the cost of fuel has skyrocketed in America, his standing with the public – stung by the higher prices at the pump and knock-on effects that led to across-the board inflation – has soured.
The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market.

It is these states – places like Iowa, Kansas, Texas and Ohio – that have become unexpected political battlegrounds in the upcoming elections that will determine if Republicans maintain control of Congress.
For months, the American president has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain.
He recently pressured European allies to further tap their oil reserves. He deferred federal taxes on the fuel and authorised supplies designated for farm use to be used in interstate trucking.
He has also promised that he would not renew attacks on Iran until after the midterms – an unusually frank acknowledgement of the political impact the ongoing conflict is having.
His decision to strike a deal with Russia's Putin is only the latest, most dramatic effort.

Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information, of course. The details of exactly how Russia is supplying this fuel to the global market, and what they might get for in return – besides much-needed hard currency – is unclear.
It opens Trump to criticism from European allies and American politicians that his administration is now helping to fund the Russian war machine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the deal a "gift" to Putin that Russia would "repay" with "terror and perfidy".
"Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged," he wrote on X.
It is also uncertain exactly how much Trump's move will help Republicans at the ballot box.
The promised European diesel release hasn't moved energy prices significantly, and there's no information on the speed with which Russian fuel could enter the market.
Its diesel refinery capacity has been damaged by repeated Ukrainian strikes – attacks that Trump has encouraged Zelensky to curtail.
The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tons this month, that amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption.
Americans may not notice much of an immediate difference.
With less than a month before November's midterm elections, early voting has already started in many states. The political cake, as the saying goes, is all but baked.
"Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in his Truth Social post.

But over the past seven months, prices on energy, fuel and consumer goods have only gone up - even as Trump and his officials have repeatedly assured an uneasy public a successful resolution to the war, and an easing of its economic impact, is nearly at hand.

Trump may be left hoping that his latest deal, setting aside its potentially uncomfortable diplomatic issues, will be enough to convince American voters that his promise of impending economic relief is more than just empty words.

articles.title: In reviewing evidence, Rodrigo Duterte's defense disputes prosecution's spreadsheet with AI summaries
articles.summary: Former President Rodrigo Duterte"s defense argued that prosecutors cannot rely on a spreadsheet containing AI-generated summaries to facilitate the review of the voluminous evidence in his case…
articles.byline: ANDY PEÑAFUERTE III, JAY-VEE MARASIGAN PANGAN

blocks.text: Published October 10, 2026 6:29am

Former President Rodrigo Duterte’s defense argued that prosecutors cannot rely on a spreadsheet containing AI-generated summaries to facilitate the review of the voluminous evidence in his case before the International Criminal Court (ICC).

In a filing made public on October 9, Duterte’s counsel Peter Haynes asked Trial Chamber III to allow them to respond to the relevance of the dataset the prosecution presented in a filing four days earlier.
The prosecution’s currently redacted dataset comprises 44,495 of the 62,034 items disclosed in Duterte’s case, as well as 8,812 of 19,241 items included on the Prosecution’s List of Evidence.

“The prosecution’s response gives the impression that the dataset is a complete archive of evidence demonstrating the number of people who were killed in police operations, as well as the deaths of drug personalities during the Presidential Period,” Haynes argued.
Duterte’s defense said the prosecution had provided a spreadsheet to help navigate thousands of documents through AI-generated summaries.
“Providing a spreadsheet to facilitate Defense navigation of thousands of documents by reliance on AI-generated summaries is no substitute for the Prosecution doing this work,” Haynes stated.

The defense argued that prosecutors were required to review the dataset in full and determine which material was incriminating, exonerating, or otherwise relevant. It also questioned what it described as the use of algorithms without human review of the content.
The defense also disputed the prosecution’s claim that the dataset underwent a “systematic and manual review”, saying the information in the dataset contradicted that claim.

“The Prosecution cannot be permitted to inflate the numbers by counting incidents in an incomplete dataset that its own provider has described as being full of irrelevant information nor having been fully reviewed,” the filing stated.
Burden to Duterte’s defense
In its October 5 filing, the prosecution asserted that it had disclosed to the defense redacted material it considered incriminating on a rolling basis.
“Items directly relevant to charged incidents were cited in the Confirmation Brief, and are cited in the Trial Brief,” the prosecution stated.

But Duterte’s lawyers are challenging that claim, and are now seeking permission from the Chamber to respond, arguing the prosecution has “mischaracterized” their position on the disclosure of material.
Haynes argued that “central background information is missing”, and that the prosecution had initially offered access to a separate platform or software with analysis capabilities.
The offer, Haynes said, was later withdrawn after the defense accepted it on July 17.
The prosecution then proposed uploading around 32,000 items to the standard DefenceJEM platform, according to the filing.

“It was proposed that this would be accompanied by an Excel spreadsheet so that the Defense could then apparently assess the relevance of each item itself and let the Prosecution know which items should be disclosed,” Haynes stated.
“This is a burden that no Defense team could or should ever accept to absorb.”
The defense also said the prosecution presented a “misleading and partial picture” of their exchanges over disclosure.

During the September 16 status conference, Haynes said the defense had also explored using artificial intelligence to deal with the voluminous evidence in the case, but found that a suitable AI tool could cost nearly half a million euros (at least P35 million).

Haynes made the remark after raising concerns about tens of thousands of documents disclosed by the prosecution. He also argued that prosecutors should have reviewed and sorted the materials before turning them over to the defense.
“We won’t assume responsibility to organize disclosed items,” Haynes said at the time.
The Chamber has yet to release a decision on the defense’s latest requests.
On October 13, the Chamber will convene the fourth status conference with the prosecution, defense, and victims’ counsel.
According to the ICC Public Affairs Unit, the Chamber expects Duterte to attend the hearing. — VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Three men found guilty of murdering Australian brothers and US friend in Mexico
articles.summary: Jake and Callum Robinson and their friend Carter Rhoad were on a surf trip when they were killed in an apparent botched robbery.

blocks.text: Three men have been found guilty of murdering Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, and their US friend Carter Rhoad during a surfing trip in Mexico in 2024.

The men's full names could not be given for legal reasons, and they were only identified as Jesús Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Ángel Jesús. They are yet to be sentenced - but are likely to spend the rest of their lives in a prison.
Debra Robinson, the brothers' mother, told the courtroom that her sons' murders had taken "the future we had imagined with them".
During the trial in the northern Baja California state, the court heard that the tourists were killed in an apparent botched robbery of their truck in a secluded beach area.
Their bodies were later found dumped down a well with gunshot wounds to their heads.
The murders sent shockwaves around the world, particularly in Australia, as the coastal area is usually safe from the violence seen in other parts of Mexico.
Debra Robinson and her husband Martin have been at the court in the coastal town of Ensenada throughout the trial, and delivered emotional testimony during closing arguments before Friday's verdict.
"It's hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons," Martin said.
Family members of Carter Rhoad joined the trial by video link.

Speaking to media outside court a week ago, Debra Robinson said the couple were "deeply grateful" to Australians for the outpouring of support they had received and that they "feel the love and their arms around us".
During the month-long trial, the prosecution had sought 150 years in prison for each of the three defendants.

In November last year, the girlfriend of the alleged ringleader, Jesús Gerardo alias "El Kekas", was sentenced in a separate trial to 20 years in prison. She had admitted to involvement in the robbery.
At the time, the murders shocked locals and tourists in Ensenada who were disturbed at the apparent ease and sheer pointlessness of the killings.
The beach town has a reputation as a welcoming spot for surfers, but the chilling murders revealed how commonplace such extreme violence remains in Mexico.
The only explanation the authorities were able to give was that the surfers - all in their early 30s - had ultimately been murdered for being in the wrong place at the wrong time.
Their killings happened barely 36 hours after they crossed into Mexico from the US. Their bodies, however, were not found for another week when their families were able to identify them.
At the time, the surfer community in Ensenada turned out in force to honour the men by paddling out at a popular surfing spot and throwing flowers into the sea.

Local surfers also called for greater security for residents and visiting tourists, citing other recent examples of violence in the state. Tourism is a key part of the regional economy in Baja California.
Amid the demands for action, state Governor Marina del Pilar Ávila tried to ease public fears about the widespread violence.
"Baja California is and will continue to be a state with safe tourism for the thousands of people who visit us from the rest of the country and the world", she said.
"I send my condolences and solidarity to the families at this difficult time."

articles.title: Controversial vaccine trial touted by RFK Jr gets go-ahead in Guinea-Bissau
articles.summary:
Recommended dose of hepatitis B vaccine will be withheld from thousands of newborns by Danish researchers

A controversial research trial that will withhold hepatitis B vaccines from some…

blocks.text: A controversial research trial that will withhold hepatitis B vaccines from some African newborns was given approval to move forward this week.
It is a central part of the vaccine vision for Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime vaccine opponent.

At an anti-vaccine conference last month, Kennedy praised the Danish researchers behind the trial and touted US-supported research on hepatitis B in newborns as exemplifying the Trump administration’s agenda for vaccines, which has included slashing vaccine recommendations and casting doubt on the safety and effectiveness of shots.
Kennedy “wants to make it so we don’t use a birth dose here in this country,” said Paul Offit, an infectious disease physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “That’s the goal.”

Kennedy would never be able to do the trial in the US because of its significant ethical concerns, Offit added. “He’s taking advantage of a developing country … Is it because children in Africa are more expendable than children here?”

Danish researchers plan to enroll 14,000 infants in Guinea-Bissau in the trial, giving the hepatitis B vaccine to half of the babies at birth and withholding it from the others for the first six weeks of life.

An ethics committee at the researchers’ home institution of the University of Southern Denmark voted this week to proceed with the trial, and officials in Guinea-Bissau have also greenlit the project, which the health minister, Quinhin Nantote, initially said was suspended after international uproar earlier this year.

Stig Børsen Hansen, a founding member who was one of two reviewers who presented the study to the Danish committee, resigned from the group in protest on Friday, citing major ethical issues with the study.

“You are now enrolling newborns in a lottery to test a hypothesis,” Hansen said. The children who are randomly selected not to receive the birth dose of the vaccine, those who “lost the lottery”, face in their earliest days the risk of contracting hepatitis B, which can cause irreversible lifelong damage. “They contract hepatitis B in the context of being part of a research project,” Hansen said, which made their infection happen, in effect, “by design”.
Three other members of the committee have also resigned in protest.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has reportedly set aside $1.6m in this year’s budget for the project, and it will be matched with private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation, which was co-founded by the billionaire activist Bill Ackman, and the Bluebell Foundation.
The CDC, the Danish researchers, Pershing Square and Nantote have not responded to the Guardian’s questions about this trial.
The news that the trial was approved by the Denmark ethics committee was first reported on Thursday by CIDRAP News. This is the first time details of the updated protocol have been disclosed.

The Guinea-Bissau study protocol has changed since it was posted in January, according to details shared with the Guardian. The researchers will now test mothers for hepatitis B before they give birth. The babies of mothers who test positive will be given the vaccine and will not be included in the trial. But the babies of mothers whose tests are negative may be enrolled. The new protocol has not been shared publicly.

In previous research, half of children who contracted hepatitis B did so after birth, through community exposures. “This virus can be transmitted casually,” Offit said. It can live on surfaces for up to seven days, and it can be acquired by sharing washcloths, toothbrushes and fingernail clippers. In addition, the hepatitis B test has a 5% false negative rate, which could provide false assurance that a birthing parent does not have the virus.

Decades of research make it clear that the vaccine would be beneficial, which means it would be unfair to place some children in the vaccinated group and some children in the unvaccinated group, said Henrik Støvring, a professor of statistics and pharmacometrics at Aarhus University in Denmark.
According to the Helsinki declaration, international medical research must be approved by ethics committees in both the host and sponsor countries.

The Danish research ethics committee at the University of Southern Denmark had never considered medical studies before, but it changed the rules in order to vote on this one. While committee members with expertise argued against approving it, the majority ruled to move forward.

“It’s very unusual to bring this into a committee like that,” Støvring said. The national ethics committee in Denmark oversees medical research, but this study was outside of their purview because it won’t take place in Denmark.

Yet “I don’t see why you couldn’t do it in Denmark,” Støvring said of the trial. In fact, several conditions make it a better location. The hepatitis B vaccine is not usually given to newborns in Denmark unless the mother is positive for the virus, for which all pregnant people are tested in Denmark.

Guinea-Bissau has some of the highest rates of hepatitis B in the world, with about 18% of adults carrying the virus. While it may be transmitted from mother to child during birth, it could also be transmitted from another parent, relatives, siblings or caregivers. Children who are infected with hepatitis B in the first year of life are significantly more likely to develop severe outcomes, including chronic infection and liver cancer.

The Bandim Health Project, run by Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, has operated in Guinea-Bissau for decades and is closely enmeshed in the country’s health system. At least one top official, the current director of public health, held a dual appointment with Bandim as recently as December.

Kennedy praised the Danish researchers at a recent anti-vaccine conference, calling them “the deities of vaccine research”. Kennedy claimed that a prior study they conducted indicated that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight.” He did not mention that another follow-up study from the same researchers found no effects at all.

This study will focus on vaccination and mortality, as well as outcomes such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. “The main problem of this trial is that you have some very well-known bad diseases that you can protect with this vaccine,” Støvring said. “And what they then want to study is something highly speculative – in a situation where WHO and others are saying that you should give this vaccine at birth, period.”

When asked about the study in a Thursday briefing, an official with the Africa CDC, which has opposed the trial, said there were “ongoing discussions” between the US and Guinea-Bissau and more details would be shared shortly. Guinea-Bissau planned to begin vaccinating all newborns against hepatitis B in 2027, but they pushed the campaign back to 2028.

Kennedy and the Danish researchers were “taking advantage of that delay in practicing standard care to put these children at risk unnecessarily”, Offit said. “What a terrible thing to do. What a horribly unethical and cruel thing to do.”

articles.title: Three men found guilty of murders of Australian surfer brothers and US friend in Mexico
articles.summary:
Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, 30 and 33, and friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were killed on a surfing trip in 2024

  • Get our

blocks.text: A Mexican judge has convicted three men of the 2024 murders of two Australian surfers and their American friend in a case that sparked international outrage.

Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33 respectively, and their friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were on a surfing trip to Mexico’s Pacific coast when they were shot dead in Baja California state in a suspected robbery.
The deaths of the trio sparked an outpouring of grief and condemnation in Australia and the United States.

Jesus Gerardo – known as “El Kekas” – was accused of leading the attack. His surname has not been disclosed for legal reasons. He and two other defendants, Irineo Francisco and Angel Jesus, were found guilty on Friday local time.
Martin and Debra Robinson, the brothers’ parents, traveled from Australia to the port city of Ensenada for the trial, which began on 7 September.
“They took our sons from our lives forever,” said Debra Robinson, who testified on the final day of the trial. “What hurts us most is that, in their final hours, they were treated with such cruelty.”
Addressing the court at the start of the trial, Martin Robinson described his sons’ murders as “hell”.
“It’s hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons,” he said.
Rhoad’s mother, Page, and his fiance, Natalie Weirtz, also participated in the hearing in a video call from the United States.
“The accused are guilty and must be punished so that no other family suffers the same pain,” Weirtz said. “Since Carter’s death, I feel paranoid and isolated.”
The surfers were camping in a remote beachside area when they were attacked in April 2024. Their bodies were found in a clifftop shaft, with gunshot wounds to their heads.

Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organised crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity does not usually affect tourists. Other foreign visitors have, however, been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast.
Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman, were killed in 2015 while traveling through the north-western state of Sinaloa. Their bodies were later burned.

articles.title: Fossil researchers believe dog-sized raptor may have fed on larger tyrannosaur
articles.summary: Researchers at the University of Alberta have made a “jaw-dropping discovery” that a raptor dinosaur may have dined on a much larger tyrannosaur.

image.caption: Joshua Doyan is a master's student in paleontology at the U of A who led the research into the bite marks. The fossils in front of the skull were a part of the research study. (Scott Neufeld/CBC)

blocks.text: Edmonton
Researchers at the University of Alberta have made a “jaw-dropping discovery” that a raptor dinosaur may have dined on a much larger tyrannosaur.
U of A researchers studied bite marks on an Albertosaurus fossil found near Drumheller, Alta.

The researchers found bite marks on the jaw of an Albertosaurus, a close relative of Tyrannosaurus rex — and often described by researchers as its “teenage cousin” — that roamed Alberta about 70 million years ago.

The fossil belonged to an eight-year-old Albertosaurus, a sub-adult that had not reached its full size. The bite marks led them to two “wildly divergent explanations” as to what happened to the dinosaur after it died near Drumheller, Alta., about 130 kilometres northeast of Calgary.
Researchers say the most likely scenario is that a raptor — a smaller, two-legged, meat-eating dinosaur — dined on the bigger Albertosaurus after it died of unknown causes.
“This is one of those rare occasions where we actually have information on a carnivore eating a carnivore,” said Philip Currie, a University of Alberta professor of dinosaur paleobiology.
“It’s a pretty big deal,” Currie added, noting that Albertosaurus was one of the dominant predators of its time.
The finding could offer new insight into how carnivorous dinosaurs interacted with one another and the complexity of the prehistoric food web.
Joshua Doyon, a master's student in paleontology at the U of A, led the research into the bite marks.
By measuring the spacing between the marks and comparing it with the teeth of other carnivorous dinosaurs that lived at the same time, researchers determined a raptor was the likeliest explanation.
The alternative hypothesis is that the Albertosaurus was cannibalized by a much younger member of its own species, less than two years old and about two metres long.
Discovery leads to research project

The fossil was discovered in 2022 by a member of the public who was canoeing and exploring the badlands north of Drumheller. The find was reported to the Royal Tyrrell Museum, which collected the specimen and prepared it by removing the surrounding rock off of the bone.
As museum staff pieced the fossil back together, they noticed the tooth marks, opening the door to Doyon's research project in 2023.
A closer view of the fossils that Doyan used in his research. (Scott Neufeld/CBC)
Doyon said he was interested in studying dinosaur behaviour and the interactions between different species when he approached museum researchers about possible projects.
The specimen offered an opportunity to investigate a feeding interaction that took place tens of millions of years ago.
Currie said the discovery highlights how paleontologists can learn more about dinosaur biology by examining details on fossils, rather than focusing only on identifying and describing the animals.
Details like the tooth marks could help researchers better understand which animals fed on others and how species interacted within prehistoric ecosystems.
Albertosaurus was an apex predator in its ecosystem, while the suspected raptor would have been much smaller — roughly comparable in size to a German shepherd, Currie said.
The finding is significant because it offers rare evidence of one carnivorous dinosaur feeding on another, rather than on prey that ate plants.
The term “raptor” can also bring to mind the dinosaurs depicted in the Jurassic Park films, but the animals found in Alberta were smaller than their Hollywood counterparts.

Doyon said the raptors that lived around Drumheller belonged to a group called dromaeosaurs. The local species, Atrociraptor, was about two metres long and considerably smaller than the dinosaurs portrayed in the movies.
Doyon said he hopes paleontologists and members of the public who find dinosaur bones will pay closer attention to small tooth marks that may otherwise go unnoticed.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jesmeen Gill is a reporter for CBC News in Edmonton. She is a graduate from Carleton University’s journalism program in Ottawa and has previously interned at The Canadian Press. You can reach her at jesmeen.gill@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Flydubai co-pilot planned suicide attack on Israeli airport, UAE prosecutors say
articles.summary:
Hammam al-Hammami is believed to have been targeting the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion airport near Tel Aviv

The co-pilot who tried to seize control of a passenger jet flying from Dubai…

blocks.text: The co-pilot who tried to seize control of a passenger jet flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv last week was planning to launch a suicide attack targeting the passenger terminal at Israel’s international airport, prosecutors in the United Arab Emirates said on Friday.

Hammam al-Hammami attacked the plane’s Indian pilot with an emergency axe, but failed to prevent his badly injured colleague from opening the cockpit’s security door to allow passengers to overpower his assailant.
Passengers then tried to control the aircraft, which was safely landed in Saudi Arabia by an off-duty relief pilot who was among about 180 passengers.

Dr Hamad Saif al-Shamsi, attorney-general of the UAE, said on Friday that al-Hammami, who is in Emirate custody, had admitted he had tried to execute a “premeditated terrorist plot to … launch a suicide attack targeting the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion airport near Tel Aviv, with the aim of causing the greatest possible loss of life”.

The 29-year-old, who was hired by flydubai, a government-owned low-cost airline, began a process of radicalisation while studying in Australia when he was influenced by the hardline takfiri ideology through reading extremist literature and online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks, al-Shamsi said in a statement.

“[Al-Hammami] subsequently developed … ideas advocating violence and terrorism. He also drew inspiration from the 11 September 2001 attacks, and the idea of carrying out a similar operation using an aircraft became firmly established in his thinking. According to his confession, this was linked to his decision to pursue a career in aviation.”

Over the weekend, Australian security agencies launched an investigation after it emerged al-Hammami spent about two years in the country as a student until 2017. He left the country without completing his engineering degree.
New Zealand authorities have launched their own investigation after police confirmed al-Hammami underwent flight training there about a year after he abandoned a degree in Australia.

There has been widespread concern about how al-Hammami was able to pass vetting and join a crew flying to Israel. An Omani national, he earned a distance-learning aviation management degree from Buckinghamshire New University in 2023 and was employed by Oman Air from 2020-24, joined Royal Air Maroc in early 2025 and worked there for several months before moving to flydubai in January 2026.

Security officials have been keen to understand if al-Hammami was acting alone or had become involved with a group such as al-Qaida or Islamic State, which could suggest further such attacks might be planned. Emirate authorities believe this is not the case.

“In the presence of his lawyer and with all legally prescribed safeguards ensured, the suspect provided a detailed confession outlining his motives and the stages of planning and execution. He admitted that he had acted alone, without the involvement of others, although investigations are continuing to verify this claim,” al-Shamsi said.
Investigators have found al-Hammami had used two previous flights to Tel Aviv to “familiarise himself with the flight route ‌and the airport”, the Emirati state news agency WAM reported.
The passengers on board the aircraft were overwhelmingly Israeli, with prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu hailing them and the pilot for their bravery after the foiled attack.

articles.title: Alberta woman, 61, breaks her own world record by planking for 5 hours
articles.summary: DonnaJean Wilde, a grandmother of 12, broke her own Guinness World Record for holding the longest female abdominal plank during the Huntsman World Senior Games in Utah this week.

image.caption: DonnaJean Wilde, 61, holds a plank at the Huntsman World Senior Games in Utah on Oct. 6. (Submitted by DonnaJean Wilde)

blocks.text: Canada·New
DonnaJean Wilde, a grandmother of 12, broke her own Guinness World Record for holding the longest female abdominal plank during the Huntsman World Senior Games in Utah this week.
DonnaJean Wilde, a grandmother of 12, says she multitasks to pass the time
You can accomplish a lot in five hours.
Fly direct from Toronto to Vancouver, for instance. Or play an entire 18-hole round of golf. Run a full marathon at an average pace. Smoke a rack of ribs.
It's an objectively long stretch of time. Now, imagine holding a plank, one of the most notoriously challenging core exercises, for the amount of time it takes to cook a Thanksgiving turkey?

"I just love it," laughed DonnaJean Wilde, who at age 61 just broke her own world record for the longest time holding an abdominal plank position (female) during the Huntsman World Senior Games in Utah this week.

Wilde is a grandmother of 12 and retired teacher from Welling, Alta. And on Tuesday, in front of a cheering crowd and several judges, she held an abdominal plank for five straight hours, shattering her previous 2024 world record of four hours, 30 minutes and 11 seconds.
Canadian woman holds plank for 5 hours, breaking world record
On Friday, she told CBC News Network she was "feeling good" and waiting for Guinness to make the record official.
"It just becomes easier to do the more repeated times you do it," Wilde said.
An abdominal plank is an isometric core exercise where you hold your body straight like a plank of wood. Most adults can hold a plank for 20 to 60 seconds, according to Health magazine.

Guinness World Records notes that to successfully achieve the record, the challenger's forearms and toes must touch the ground at all times. "The remainder of the body must be lifted off the ground and be kept straight throughout."
Not her only world record
Wilde says she started planking about 15 years ago when she broke her arm and was looking for a way to stay fit.
"I love to work out. I love fitness, and I discovered I could plank with a cast on," she said.

items: Walk fast, live longer? McMaster University researchers say walking speed is an important health indicator
Fitness influencer apologizes after hitching a bike ride in the Berlin Marathon

blocks.text: "And when the cast came off, it became a habit that I actually embraced and fell in love with."

When she first started, she says she could hold a plank for about a minute or minute and a half, but she kept practicing. With her family's encouragement, she kept going and minutes became hours. By 2024, she broke the Guinness World Record.

Wilde, seen in the midst of achieving her latest world record, says that while she holds her hours-long planks she likes to multitask: reading, writing and earning her master's. (Submitted by DonnaJean Wilde)

And, for good measure, she broke a second one that year by completing 1,575 pushups in one hour — the most push ups in one hour (female). She told the Guinness World Records she fell in love with doing pushups while doing 500 every day as training for her planks.
Now, she planks every day for at least a few hours. But it doesn't eat into her time, she says. She multitasks.
"Just read, do texts, whatever, do schoolwork. I did a master's degree while I was planking. Wrote a book," she said.
The book, From Minutes To Hours: I Wrote This Book While Planking, came out last year.
CBC News did not attempt to write this story while planking.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Natalie Stechyson has been a writer and editor at CBC News since 2021. She covers stories on social trends, families, gender, human interest, as well as general news. She's worked as a journalist since 2009, with stints at the Globe and Mail and Postmedia News, among others. Before joining CBC News, she was the parents editor at HuffPost Canada, where she won a silver Canadian Online Publishing Award for her work on pregnancy loss. You can reach her at natalie.stechyson@cbc.ca.

articles.title: In U-turn on U.S. pressure on Russia, Trump says Washington to buy diesel from Moscow
articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump said that he has struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, a stunning reversal of years of U.S. pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine and an attempt to address…

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump announced on social media Friday that he has struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia. (Evan Vucci/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

U.S. President Donald Trump said that he has struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, a stunning reversal of years of U.S. pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine and an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.
U.S. has not imported Russian oil or gas since 2022, following Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine
Trump said on social media Friday that he struck the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call in which he was expected to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia.

Instead, Trump announced that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and one million tons "immediately thereafter." Russia will deliver another three million tons "within a short period of time" after that, he wrote.
Had signed sweeping sanctions law

Trump's shocking announcement comes after he signed a sweeping Russia sanctions law last month that aimed at clamping down on Russia's energy economy, among other areas, that fuel its war against Ukraine.
War in Ukraine is at a dangerous stalemate, says U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio

His move casts doubt on the likelihood of the White House imposing sanctions on Russia this month, given that a bipartisan law passed by Congress directs the administration to target the top importers of Russian oil and gas.
Trump, in his announcement, did not address the sanctions or Russia's war but said, "Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority."
Details not immediately clear

The White House did not immediately respond to questions about who was paying for the diesel from Russia and when the fuel being supplied under the agreement would become available. It also did not clarify whether subsequent supplies of Russian diesel set to come next month would be supplied prior to Election Day on Nov. 3.
Trump said on social media that he'd struck the diesel-related deal after speaking to Russian President Vladimir Putin. (Gavriil Grigorov/Sputnik/The Associated Press)
Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev reposted the Treasury Department's announcement on X Friday and said that "Russia-US co-operation on diesel and energy will benefit the world."
The law Trump signed last month envisions sanctions on Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers and bans all new U.S. investment in Russia and the handling of sovereign debt.

It also directed Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15 per cent of Russia's natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.
Bans began under Biden
The U.S. has not imported Russian oil or gas since 2022, when the Biden administration banned them because of Moscow's invasion of Ukraine, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
Shortly after Trump made the announcement, the U.S. Treasury Department said it was immediately issuing a temporary licence allowing Russian diesel to be supplied to the global market.

Gas prices globally have surged as the war in Iran upends the energy sector. The national average for a gallon of diesel in the U.S. was $6.23 US on Friday, according to AAA, after hitting a record $6.52 US on Sept. 22.

articles.title: After days of giving French-only answers in legislature, Kinew wants schools to cover '80s language battle
articles.summary: Manitoba's premier wants the province's schools to teach students about the intense public backlash to the expansion of francophone rights in the 1980s.

image.caption: Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew, seen here in an August file photo, says schools should teach students about the French-language crisis of the 1980s, when a bill calling for provincial government services to be offered in French sparked an outcry and protests. (Jeff Stapleton/CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba
Manitoba's premier wants the province's schools to teach students about the intense public backlash to the expansion of francophone rights in the 1980s.
Premier says kids should learn about 'struggles and challenges' to preserve francophone culture in Manitoba
Manitoba's premier wants the schools in the province to teach students about the bitter fight against the expansion of francophone rights in the 1980s.

Premier Wab Kinew is calling for the addition to the education curriculum, after his decision to speak almost exclusively in French during four days of question period at the legislature was celebrated by some and questioned by others.
He also said he'd like to see a live French-to-English translation of question period offered for people watching online — which the legislative assembly is working on.

"I hope that after this week, we can use this experience as motivation to renew our education system to share our own history as Manitoba, including those struggles and challenges for the Francophonie to protect your language and your culture," Kinew told host Jérémy Laniel in a Friday French-language interview with Le 6 à 9, Radio-Canada's morning radio show in Manitoba.

Kinew was referring to the French-language crisis of the 1980s, when a government bill calling for provincial services to be offered in French sparked an outcry and protests from some English-speakers.

items: Manitoba premier's French-only answers in question period 'unhealthy' politicizing of language: academic

blocks.text: The offices of the Société de la francophonie manitobaine were targeted by an arson, and the opposition Progressive Conservatives spent nearly two weeks blocking a vote on the government bill.
The NDP government succumbed to the public pressure, withdrawing the bill in 1984.
By the next year, however, the Supreme Court of Canada ruled Manitoba's unilingual laws were unconstitutional. The laws needed to be translated into French to be re-enacted, the court ruled.
Kinew said many Manitobans aren't aware of this history.

"The reality in Manitoba is that the French language is the language of your mothers, your fathers, your grandparents. And then they had to hide their books, they had to hide their signs with French text," he said in French.

Kinew said the government would consult with the Franco-Manitoban School Division, Société de la francophonie manitobaine and other experts who understand that history before incorporating it into the curriculum.
Bernard Lesage, board chair of the French-language school division, said he's pleased that if the changes are approved, all students will get to learn more about Franco-Manitoban history.
Criticized for French answers

Since La Vérendrye MLA Konrad Narth was appointed interim leader of the Opposition Progressive Conservatives two weeks ago, Kinew has answered every English-language question put to him in the legislature in French.
In late May, Narth — who doesn't speak French — got into hot water when he was overheard saying Kinew showed a "basic lack of respect" for responding to his question in French.
Narth later said he asked the question in English, not French, prompting heckling from NDP MLAs who accused him of disrespecting the language, according to an audio recording of the exchange.

He later apologized for how his comments came across. Narth also said he appreciates that he can ask questions in the language he's most comfortable in, and Kinew can respond in French with translation available to all MLAs.
The premier has denied that he's speaking French in the chamber because of Narth's actions from May. He told reporters this week Narth was "disrespecting the bilingual tradition."

Interim Progressive Conservative Leader Konrad Narth said this week he has no issues with the premier speaking in French in the chamber. Narth doesn't speak French, but can listen to a live translation in the chamber. (Kevin Nepitabo/CBC)
By Friday, Kinew suggested he feels "a bit like Forrest Gump" — the movie character famed for going on an epic cross-country run "for no particular reason."
Kinew said he started speaking French, "and then I thought it was important to keep going. But I don't really know the exact reason."
Kinew has previously spoken French in the legislature but usually only regarding francophone matters.
Boosting national profile: political scientist
He disagreed Friday that he is politicizing the use of French, as Raymond Hébert, a professor emeritus of political studies who wrote a book on Manitoba's French-language crisis, has suggested.
Hébert also said the premier's conduct might undermine his government's efforts to advance bilingualism by antagonizing anglophones.
Kinew said he respects Hébert, but "Manitoba has changed a lot," pointing to growth in French-immersion schools and the many people who speak and respect the language and its history.
His NDP government has vowed to make the province a "truly bilingual" province. The province consulted with people last year, and a provincial strategy is scheduled for release in March 2027.

While Manitoba's courts and legislature operate in English and French, other government services are offered in both languages only in designated areas where there is a "concentrated" francophone population. The province is not officially bilingual by law.

items: The NDP wants Manitoba to be 'truly bilingual.' What does that mean?

blocks.text: A political scientist in Quebec suggested Kinew's use of French in the legislature may be about more than scoring political points or appealing to Franco-Manitobans.

"I think that is someone who might have national ambitions, and certainly someone who has a national profile" as a popular premier, said Daniel Béland, director of the McGill Institute for the Study of Canada.
"Showing to the rest of the country, and including to people in Quebec, that he speaks French … increases his profile across the country."
Kinew also told Radio-Canada he doesn't think it "would be a huge deal" to offer live translation of question period. MLAs already receive a translation through an earpiece on their desks.
He said those decisions are up to the legislature's Speaker, who, earlier this year, made picture-in-picture American Sign Language interpretation available during all question period broadcasts.

Rick Yarish, clerk of the legislative assembly, said the legislature doesn't currently have the technological capacities to provide the translation but is working to implement the service. No timeline is available.

He said the goal is to have a second video feed of question period airing exclusively on the assembly's broadcast page, which would include a live French-to-English translation. The primary video feed, featuring whichever language is being spoken, would remain as is and broadcast simultaneously on YouTube.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Ian Froese covers the Manitoba Legislature and provincial politics for CBC News in Winnipeg. He serves as president of the legislature's press gallery. He studied U.S. culture, media and politics as a 2025 World Press Institute fellow. You can reach him at ian.froese@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Vance unsure if Pentagon will livestream a prisoner's execution, but he won't be watching
articles.summary: U.S. Vice President JD Vance said on Friday he does not know whether the Pentagon will carry out its plan to livestream the execution by firing squad of the former U.S. Army psychiatrist convicted in…

image.caption: U.S. Vice-President JD Vance, seen above in Lima, Ohio, on Friday, says he will not watch the execution of a prisoner that the Pentagon says will be streamed live. (Samuel Corum/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New

U.S. Vice President JD Vance said on Friday he does not know whether the Pentagon will carry out its plan to livestream the execution by firing squad of the former U.S. Army psychiatrist convicted in the deadly 2009 Fort Hood shooting, a plan that has drawn broad condemnation.
Trump has not said whether he thinks execution should be shown on a livestream

U.S. Vice-President JD Vance said Friday he does not know whether the Pentagon will carry out its plan to livestream the firing-squad execution of the former U.S. Army psychiatrist convicted in the deadly 2009 Fort Hood shooting, a proposal that has drawn broad condemnation.

As the controversy over the plan championed by U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth grew, ‌former U.S. officials warned that livestreaming the execution would hand terrorists a recruiting tool, while a top U.S. Catholic bishop called the plan "barbaric."
"I don't know that that's actually going to happen," Vance told reporters in Cincinnati, referring to the livestream.
Vance added that if the Dec. 3 execution is livestreamed, "I'm not going to be watching it."
Firing squad execution to be livestreamed, Pentagon says

Vance's comments raise questions about support within U.S. President Donald Trump's administration to the Pentagon's plan to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, who was found guilty in a U.S. military trial of killing ​13 people at Fort Hood in Texas.

Trump said at a White House event Friday that Hasan deserves the ​death penalty by firing squad, calling him "a maniac." The Republican president has not said whether he thinks the execution should be livestreamed.
Death penalty experts said it would mark the first known broadcast or livestream of a lawful execution.

items: Pentagon says firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamed
The U.S. plans to livestream an execution. Here's how that compares to global practice

blocks.text: Hegseth, a Trump appointee, said Thursday that the public nature of the execution would demonstrate "there's serious consequences for these ​types of things."
Hegseth reposted a comment Trump made in 2013, possibly about the Boston Marathon bombers, saying: "Should be public execution for all to see — you will end this ⁠bullshit fast!"

The Pentagon on Friday declined to say whether ⁠families of those killed in Hasan's attack would be invited to attend the execution, as is common practice in civilian ‌executions. It also remains unclear how the Army would select the shooters and what protocols would be followed. The Pentagon said it would release details later.
'Barbaric promotion of a culture of death'
A top U.S. Catholic official condemned the plan.
"This decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered," said Archbishop Paul Coakley, president of the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops.
U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth shakes hands with U.S. President Donald Trump during an event in Sparrows Point, Maryland, earlier this month. (Jim Watson/AFP/Getty Images)
The Catholic Church opposes capital punishment. Vance, a convert to Catholicism, has written a book about his faith.

Hegseth, a member of a conservative evangelical denomination, has invoked Christian language when discussing the Iran war and ⁠has led prayer services at the Pentagon. Hegseth also brushed off Pope Leo's criticism of the war.

Hasan is set to become the first person executed by firing squad by the U.S. military since 1945. Hasan, an American-born Muslim, said during his 2013 trial that he carried out the shootings to try to stop what he called a U.S. war on Islam.
"Whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this ‌is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people," Vance told reporters.
Gift to 'terrorist recruiters': senator
Joe Kent, who resigned this year as Trump's head of the U.S. National Counterterrorism Center, said the effort to deter extremism by livestreaming the execution could backfire.
"Streaming his execution is not just a stain on our morality — it also gives the terrorists free propaganda that they will use to radicalize & recruit more terrorists," Kent wrote on social media.

Republican Sen. Thom Tillis wrote on social media that Hasan should be put to death, but that livestreaming his execution would be "beyond disgusting" and something that "oppressive dictatorships like Iran and ​Afghanistan do."

items: U.S. army moves to execute man convicted in 2009 deadly Fort Hood rampage by firing squad
Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan sentenced to death

blocks.text: Sen. Jack Reed, the top Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee and a former Army officer, said such a livestream would give Hasan more attention.
"This is a gift to anti-American terrorist recruiters. It is absolutely shameful and damaging to America's interests and core values," Reed said in a statement.
The ⁠UN human rights office condemned the decision.

"Public executions constitute a form of cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment," Shabia Mantoo, a spokesperson for the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, told a news briefing in ⁠Geneva.
Mantoo added that it would "breach the absolute prohibition of torture."
Heightened debate over death penalty

The decision to livestream the execution comes amid heightened debate in the United States over the death penalty following the botched lethal ⁠injection last week ⁠of a Tennessee woman who was sentenced to death for a 1995 murder. ​

The controversy has also flared in the run-up to the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections, with polls indicating Trump's party could lose control of the U.S. House of Representatives and possibly the U.S. Senate to the Democrats.

The execution is scheduled to take place at the same sprawling military base where Hasan opened fire ⁠with a handgun in a medical facility. A military jury sentenced him to death after finding him guilty of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder.

The shooting came weeks before Hasan, now 56, was scheduled to deploy with U.S. forces to Afghanistan. Hasan was left partially paralyzed and confined to a wheelchair from being shot by police during his arrest.
The group Death Penalty Action, which opposes capital punishment, said Hasan's execution would be the first U.S. military execution since 1961, which was carried out by hanging.
The last known executions by U.S. military firing squads took place in 1945, the Death Penalty Information Center said.

At least five states have firing squads on the books, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. In ⁠2025, South Carolina carried out the first such execution in the United States ‌in 15 years.

articles.title: 'Crypto King' investor recounts the moment he learned $311M investment fund didn’t exist
articles.summary: An investor and friend of Aiden Pleterski showed up at the lakefront mansion of the self-described "Crypto King" in June 2022 to "get proof in person" of how much money was in Pleterski’s investment…

image.caption: Mitchell Learning, a friend of 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski, took the stand Friday, on the fourth day of Pleterski’s fraud and money laundering trial in Toronto. (Mehrdad Nazarahar/CBC)

blocks.text: Toronto

An investor and friend of Aiden Pleterski showed up at the lakefront mansion of the self-described "Crypto King" in June 2022 to "get proof in person" of how much money was in Pleterski’s investment account. Pleterski has pleaded not guilty to fraud over $5,000 and money laundering.
Mitchell Learning testified on 4th day of trial that Aiden Pleterski admitted to running 'Ponzi scheme'

An investor and friend of Aiden Pleterski showed up at the lakefront mansion of the self-described "Crypto King" in June 2022 to "get proof in person" of how much money was in Pleterski’s investment account — after receiving a screenshot and video showing a balance of $311 million.

Mitchell Learning, who said he invested $400,000, took the stand Friday, on the fourth day of Pleterski’s fraud and money laundering trial in Toronto. Both the screenshot and video showing the trading account were presented in Superior Court.
Pleterski wasn’t home when Learning arrived at his Burlington, Ont., home.

In his absence, Learning testified he was able to gain access to Pleterski’s email account on his computer and found an email from the trading platform FXChoice confirming Pleterski had "successfully deleted" the account where the $311 million was supposed to be.

Aiden Pleterski's Burlington, Ont., mansion. Friend and investor Mitchell Learning, who said he invested $400,000 with Pleterski, says he went to his home seeking proof of an investment fund. (Pelin Sidki/CBC)

He then told mutual friends to come to Pleterski’s mansion, and one of them recorded a video, also presented in court, of Pleterski’s emails. Those included account statements from another trading platform Forex.com.
"Looks like it’s never been higher than $1,000, oh my god," the friend says on the video as he and Learning look through the statements.
Referring to the "available margin" on another statement, the friend says, "400 f–king dollars, I’ve been f–ked."
Confronting the 'Crypto King'

Later, Learning said Pleterski returned home and told him and Pleterski’s girlfriend "a story" where Pleterski was trading and everything was going well until the summer of 2021 "where apparently things took a turn."
"At the end of the summer, around September 2021, he had $40 million in a trading account," Learning said about what Pleterski told him.
"It only kept going down from there. He tried to make riskier trades to make money back, essentially losing the remainder of the money and then from that point on starting running a Ponzi scheme."
Mitchell Learning testified at the Superior Court in Toronto on Friday on the fourth day of 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski’s fraud and money laundering trial. (Pam Davies/CBC News)
Afterward, Learning said he left the house and didn’t really know what to do.
"There were a lot of emotions and I was definitely very upset about everything," he said in court.
Two days later, Learning said he recorded a phone call with Pleterski. The jury was expected to hear that recording after lunch Friday.

items: 'Crypto King' investor who lost $890K recounts visit to Aiden Pleterski’s lakefront mansion

blocks.text: The Crown is alleging Pleterski guaranteed investors' money given to him for trading, but never actually invested the funds. Instead, the Crown argues Pleterski spent the money on himself, including on exotic cars, flights on private jets, lavish shopping and credit card bills that ran into the millions.
Range Rover, McLaren on Instagram

Earlier Friday, Learning explained how he first met Pleterski when they played a season of baseball together in 2014. They followed each other on Instagram, and in 2020 when Learning saw Pleterski post a photo of Range Rover and McLaren, Learning said he reached out to find out what Pleterski was up to. Pleterski said he was trading.
In Sept. 2020, Learning first gave Pleterski $2,500 to trade on his behalf. His investment later grew to $400,000.
"I got quite a lot of money out originally," said Learning. "I think it was just over a million dollars."
Aiden Pleterski posted these photos from the Burlington, Ont., mansion where he was living on his Instagram account. (aiden.ptrs/Instagram)
Learning testified that he eventually gave some of that money to family and friends who also invested and were trying to get their principal funds back.

Earlier on, Learning also said he tried to get more involved in Pleterski’s operation and would pick up and deliver bank drafts from investors for Pleterski, at one point getting paid $2,000 a week for six weeks to do these and similar errands.

Learning also went on three trips with Pleterski, where they flew on private jets — one to Ohio for a boxing match, a second to Florida for a week and a third to Turks and Caicos for Pleterski’s girlfriend’s birthday in March 2022.

items: 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski will represent himself at his fraud trial

blocks.text: Pleterski was arrested in May 2024 after a lengthy investigation by Durham Regional Police and the Ontario Securities Commission. Police allege he operated a multimillion-dollar Ponzi scheme. He’s pleaded not guilty to fraud over $5,000 and money laundering.
So far at trial, nine investors have testified to giving Pleterski more than $2 million collectively to trade on their behalf. Most of them said they didn’t get any of that money back.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Nicole Brockbank is a reporter for CBC Toronto's Enterprise Unit. She digs up, researches and reports GTA-focused investigative and enterprise stories. nicole.brockbank@cbc.ca

articles.title: Schools crisis in France: Investment fails to inspire confidence
articles.summary: For weeks, schoolchildren in France have been protesting the failing education system. Compared to many other countries, France invests heavily in education but critics say that the funds are not…

image.caption: University students have joined in on the protests to support schoolchildrenImage: Christophe Agostinis/MAXPPP/picture alliance

blocks.text: Rats in the toilets, leaking roofs, broken heating systems: Cellphone videos filmed by French schoolchildren and circulating on social media bear witness to the dilapidated infrastructure in many educational institutions across France.

At the Lycee Paul Eluard in the Parisian suburb of Saint-Denis, a center of the current protests, young people have reported that there are vermin in the building, and say burst pipes are a regular occurrence. In nearby Pantin, pupils complained that windows couldn't be opened, even when temperatures soared to 40 degrees Celsius (over 104 degrees Fahrenheit) in summer.
Pupils also complain of overcrowded classrooms and frequently cancelled lessons.
The protests, which have erupted all over the country, show no sign of coming to an end.
France students demand better schools
Problems of centralization

Yet, by EU standards, France invests a substantial amount in its education system — 6.7% of its GDP. The fact that this investment has not translated into a better learning environment may be partly attributable to the way responsibilities are divided.

The central government in Paris mainly deals with paying teachers, and setting national curricula. But the responsibility for maintaining school buildings lies with France's various levels of local government. For elementary schools, the administration responsible is the municipality; for "colleges" (lower secondary schools, ages 11–15) it is the wider department, and for lycees (upper secondary schools, ages 15–18) it is the region.

Depending on the region, the local authorities have different financial possibilities at their disposal, and must plan renovation projects themselves. Progress on making improvements is often very slow as a result. In addition, more than two-thirds of their budget is already allocated to staffing costs and pension payments, leaving relatively little room for investment.
Dilapidated infrastructure

Over 80% of elementary school buildings in France are more than 50 years old. An estimated 10 to 20% of all school buildings are considered to be in serious need of renovation. In many instances, politicians have been trying to address the problem. Ile-de-France, which covers Paris and the region surrounding it, approved a 10-year program of renovation and expansion for the period 2017 to 2027 at a cost of €6.6 billion ($7.4 billion).

According to the local authorities, two-thirds of upper secondary pupils now attend a new school, or one that has been renovated. But even after mold has been removed and roofs repaired, it is still rare for buildings to have effective protection against the summer heat. It is also a bitter irony that some buildings newly constructed at considerable expense, or renovated just a few years earlier, have been damaged in the recent protests.
France students protest school conditions
Macron tried in vain to address problem

Imbalances are also evident in ongoing education expenditure. While France invests a comparatively large amount in upper secondary education, according to OECD calculations Paris spends less per primary school pupil than the average for industrialized countries. Education researchers emphasize that it is precisely these early years that lay the foundation for subsequent academic success.

The governments put in place by French President Emmanuel Macron have attempted to address this imbalance. Since 2017, class sizes in the first years of primary school have been halved in socially disadvantaged areas, and around 16,000 additional teaching posts created.

Amid the ongoing protests, the government has said it now intends to recruit more than 3,000 supply teachers at short notice. French Education Minister Edouard Geffray announced that software would be used to identify schools that are in a particularly difficult situation.

These announcements are the government's first concrete response to the demands of the students, who have been demonstrating for almost two weeks now, calling for better facilities in secondary schools, more supply teachers and greater investment in the education system generally.

blocks.caption: Schoolchildren and students all over France have joined in on the protestsImage: Stephane Mahe/REUTERS

blocks.text: Increasing deficiencies

The latest scores for the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development’s (OECD) program for international student assessment (Pisa), which were published in September, illustrate the scale of the problems in the education system. According to the results, more than one in three 15-year-olds in France no longer achieve a basic level of competence in mathematics, for example.

Macron's reform of the upper secondary education system has also been criticized. The abolition of academic streaming in favor of specialist subjects selected by the individual was meant to give pupils greater freedom of choice. However, the large number of possible subject combinations make it difficult to timetable lessons. Students complain that they have too many free periods and longer school days.

The problems also extend to universities. A lecturer at a Paris university described a seminar attended by 50 students — so many that they have to fetch chairs from other rooms or sit on the floor. So far, she said, the university administration had done nothing about it.

blocks.caption: Pupils and students in Bron, a suburb of Lyon, called for better learning conditions and investment in the education systemImage: Pittore/NEIRDAPROD/SIPA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Cancelled lessons

Compared with pupils in other EU countries, French schoolchildren have a high number of teaching hours per school year — on paper, at least. But the French Court of Accounts recorded that 9% of lessons at state colleges were cancelled in the 2023–24 school year. A study from the school year 2024–25 suggests that only around 12% of lessons cancelled at short notice are covered by other teachers.

The relatively low salaries of French teachers compared to those in neighboring countries are also a problem. OECD data shows that after 15 years in the profession teachers at lower secondary schools in France only earn about half as much as their German counterparts.
Broken promises of equality

France takes pride in its republican model of education, which is supposed to provide all children with equal opportunities, irrespective of their background. In reality, academic success in France is much more dependent on parents' socioeconomic circumstances than in many other countries. This is also apparent in that children from poorer families are far more likely to be affected by the cancellation of lessons.

The government's financial room for maneuver is currently restricted by the country's precarious budgetary situation. Although the draft budget for 2027 includes an additional €1.2 billion for the Ministry of Education, there are also plans to cut teaching posts, on the grounds that pupil numbers are falling.

blocks.caption: Students also protested against the media coverage of the problems in the education systemImage: Raphael Lafargue/abaca/picture alliance

blocks.text: Protests in the run-up to the presidential election

It's not just videos of dilapidated school buildings that are circulating on social media. As the discontent has spread, there is also footage of demonstrations where people carry placards with political slogans that have little to do with education policy. Some videos show burning barricades and clashes with the police, which faces accusations of usingdisproportionate force.

blocks.caption: Saint-Denis mayor, Bally Bagayoko, tried to shield student protesters from riot police Image: Kenzo Tribouillard/AFP

blocks.text: Some members of the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) party have associated themselves with the protesting students. Lawmakers have appeared at school blockades and shared related videos. The government has accused LFI of deliberately exploiting young people's anger for political purposes, an allegation that the party rejects.
With the French presidential election just six months away, the protests over the crisis in education are evolving into a power struggle.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Thai Queen makes first solo flight in fighter jet
articles.summary: Thailand’s Queen Suthida made her first solo flight in a fighter jet, according to the Thai Royal Household.

blocks.text: Thailand's Queen Suthida made her first solo flight in a fighter jet, according to the Thai Royal Household.
The Queen was shown boarding a Gripen on 8 October at an airfield in Surat Thani province, southern Thailand, while King Maha Vajiralongkorn watched from the ground.
The Royal Household has said she is an experienced pilot, having logged about 1,188 hours across several types of aircraft since she began flying in 2010.
She also co-piloted aircraft carrying the King on official visits to other countries, the Royal Household said.

articles.title: Powerful magnitude 7.7 earthquake hits Panama, damaging buildings
articles.summary: Tsunami warnings are issued for neighbouring countries as videos of destruction circulate online.

blocks.text: A massive magnitude 7.7 earthquake has hit Panama, damaging buildings and prompting a wide-ranging tsunami warning for neighbouring countries.

About 4.6 million people felt moderate to severe shaking as a result of the quake, according to the US Geological Survey, which has said that the effects of the disaster were "likely to be widespread".
The quake, which hit just before 15:00 local time (18:00 GMT), could trigger tsunamis in Colombia, Costa Rica, Chile and Mexico, according to the US Tsunami Warning System.
The epicentre of the earthquake was about 6.2 miles (10km) from the small town of Pitaloza Arriba in south-central Panama, with a series of shallow aftershocks following it.
Footage shared online, which has not been verified by the BBC, appears to show collapsed buildings in the towns of Penonomé and Soná.
The quake was registered as occurring at a depth of just 12km. The shallower the earthquake, the more likely it is to have more severe effects on the surface.
However, the full extent of the damage it has caused is not yet clear, nor whether there have been any casualties as a result.
Many people were evacuated from buildings in Panama City, about 200km (124 miles) away, according to new agency AFP.
The earthquake comes just three days before Panama was scheduled to hold a national evacuation drill for dealing with a major earthquake.
It also follows devastating earthquakes in Colombia and Venezuela earlier this year.

articles.title: Trump, Putin agree on deal to release Russian diesel to US, world markets
articles.summary: Russia will supply diesel to global markets in a bid to lower prices, US President Donald Trump has said. The move reverses years of pressure on the Russian economy following the Russian invasion of…

image.caption: Trump said he expected the influx of Russian diesel to lower fuel pricesImage: Sascha Thelen/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump announced on Friday an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin for the release of Russian diesel to global markets, which marks a dramatic turnaround in US policy toward Moscow since the start of the war in Ukraine.
The move also aims to address rising fuel costs before the US midterm elections.
In a social media post, Trump wrote he had made a deal with Putin during a phone call that was supposed to be about a suspected plague outbreak in Russia.
What did Trump say?
According to Trump, Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter."
Trump wrote that Russia would deliver another 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that.
The US Treasury Department issued a temporary license that will allow Russian diesel to reach global markets through April 2027.
Sanctions against Russia
Since its 2022 full-scale invasion of neighboring Ukraine, Moscow has been hit with waves of sanctions by the United States and its partners.
Earlier this year, temporary US sanctions waivers that allowed the sale of Russian oil raised concerns because they could hinder efforts to deprive Moscow of funds for its war in Ukraine.
Trump's announcement on Friday came just before US, Ukrainian, and European officials were set to meet in Miami for new diplomatic talks aimed at ending Russia's war in Ukraine.
